The 363 mile canal linking Lake Erie at Buffalo to the Hudson River at Albany opened fully in October 1825, after eight years of digging that used no engineers trained in canal building, since none existed yet in the United States. Its 83 locks lifted boats past Niagara's drop in elevation without any need to portage around the falls.

New York state funded the project after Congress and other states declined, and tolls repaid the construction cost within about a decade. Freight rates between the Midwest and the Atlantic coast fell sharply once it opened, and the canal is widely credited with helping make New York City the country's dominant port over rivals like Philadelphia and Baltimore.

Water clocks had existed for centuries by 725, but they drifted, because a steady flow of water is hard to hold constant. Yi Xing, a Buddhist monk and astronomer, and the engineer Liang Lingzan solved that for the Tang court by adding a mechanism that let a wheel advance only in fixed, regulated steps rather than turning freely.

That regulator, an escapement, is the same basic idea that governs a mechanical clock centuries later in Europe, though no direct link between the two has been shown. Their device drove an armillary sphere and a rotating globe modelling the sky, with bells and drums sounding automatically to mark the hours, built for a court concerned with astronomy and calendar-keeping rather than everyday timekeeping.

Philip II commissioned El Escorial partly to fulfil a vow made after a battlefield victory on Saint Lawrence's feast day, and the complex combines a monastery, a royal palace, a library and a mausoleum for Spanish monarchs in one severe granite building outside Madrid. Construction ran from 1563 and was completed in 1584, though Philip kept adding to its library and art collection afterward.

Philip governed much of his empire from a small, plainly furnished room there with a direct view into the church, choosing austerity over the ornament typical of royal residences elsewhere in Europe. Spanish monarchs have been buried in its crypt since his own death in 1598.

The eleven churches at Lalibela were carved downward rather than built up: masons cut trenches into volcanic rock, then hollowed a monolithic building from the block left standing before tunnelling out interior rooms, windows and altars. Tradition credits King Lalibela, who ruled Ethiopia's Zagwe dynasty from around 1181 to 1221.

Some construction, judged from the site's layout, likely continued into the early 1200s rather than finishing within his reign alone. Ethiopian Orthodox Christians still hold services in the churches, and pilgrims climb narrow rock cut passages between them each January during Christmas celebrations there.

On 1 December 1990, Englishman Graham Fagg and Frenchman Philippe Cozette shook hands through a small hole in the service tunnel, 40 metres beneath the seabed of the English Channel, the first physical link between mainland Britain and continental Europe since the ice age. Television crews on both sides broadcast the moment live.

Boring had started from Folkestone and Sangatte in 1988 using huge rotating cutter heads, and the two drives met within centimetres of their planned line despite running for years without direct contact. The breakthrough came four years before passenger and freight trains actually began running through the finished tunnel in 1994.

Edgar Kaufmann Jr. expected a house with a view of the waterfall on his family's land. Frank Lloyd Wright built the house on top of it instead, cantilevering concrete terraces directly over the falling water so the sound would be part of living there, a decision the family's own engineers warned might not hold.

Those engineers were closer to right than Wright admitted. The cantilevers sagged over the following decades from underbuilt reinforcement, and a 2002 restoration had to add steel supports beneath the terraces to stop further deflection without changing how the house looks from outside.

Edith Farnsworth commissioned a weekend retreat and got a glass box on steel stilts above a flood plain in Plano, Illinois. Mies van der Rohe designed it with almost no interior walls and floor to ceiling glass on every side, an idea he had been refining since the 1920s, finally built full size for a client who could afford to indulge it.

Farnsworth and Mies fell out badly over cost overruns and eventually sued each other; she later called the house unlivable, too hot in summer and too exposed to insects and passers by. The house has flooded repeatedly since, and its owners have had to raise it and its furnishings to protect it from the Fox River.

George Ferris, a bridge engineer, built his wheel for the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago after organisers challenged American designers to produce something to rival the Eiffel Tower from four years earlier. His wheel stood 80 metres tall, carried 36 wooden cars each holding up to 60 people, and turned on the largest axle forged up to that time.

Around 1.4 million people rode it over the fair's run, each trip lasting about twenty minutes for two full revolutions. Ferris never profited much from the ride; disputes with the exposition's organisers over the fees ate into his earnings, and the original wheel was dismantled and later scrapped after a second fair in St. Louis in 1904.

Flax stems will not yield usable fibre on their own; the stalk has to be broken down first. Retting, soaking bundles of harvested flax in water so bacteria rot away the pectin binding fibre to woody core, is attested by retting pits and flax remains found at Egyptian sites, alongside tomb paintings showing the crop pulled, bundled and soaked before further work.

After retting, hackling, drawing the stems through a bed of fixed pins or spikes, combed out the broken woody core and separated long fibres from short ones. Egyptian linen prized for its fineness, some of it found wrapping mummies, depended on this two stage process. Neither step left a single named inventor; both are known from the tools, remains and depictions that Egyptian sites preserved.

The Kalendrier des Bergers, printed in Paris around 1491, mixed a calendar of saints' days and lunar phases with medical advice, moral tales and crude woodcuts aimed at a rural audience rather than scholars. Its French title translates as the shepherd's calendar, and later editions in English and other languages kept that pastoral framing even after the book had spread to city readers who had never kept sheep.

Its practical mix of weather lore, bloodletting charts tied to the zodiac and short verse made it one of the most reprinted books of its century, passing through countless editions across Europe. That format, a cheap yearly guide to the sky and the body sold alongside proverbs, set the pattern almanacs followed for the next three hundred years.

The Aqua Claudia was begun under Caligula and finished by Claudius in 52 CE, carrying water some 69 kilometres from springs near Subiaco into Rome, most of it underground and only the final stretch raised onto the arches that still stand along the Appian Way. It was one of the four aqueducts the Romans themselves ranked as their finest.

It was not Rome's first aqueduct. That was the Aqua Appia, built in 312 BCE, over three and a half centuries earlier and almost entirely underground for secrecy and protection. The Claudia's raised arcade became the more visible symbol of Roman engineering because so much more of its above-ground structure survived intact.

Abraham Ortelius, a map dealer and engraver in Antwerp, published the Theatrum Orbis Terrarum in 1570 as a bound set of 53 uniformly styled maps rather than the loose sheets most buyers were used to purchasing separately. The word 'atlas' for a map collection came slightly later, from Gerardus Mercator's own volume, but Ortelius's book set the format that made the term stick.

Ortelius kept revising the work through dozens of later editions, adding new maps as fresh surveys and voyages reported them, so no single printing shows a fixed final version. It sold well enough across Europe to make him wealthy, and copies of the earliest editions are now rare enough to sell at auction for sums few sixteenth-century mapmakers could have imagined.

KDKA, a Westinghouse station in Pittsburgh, began broadcasting on 2 November 1920 from a makeshift studio, reading returns from the Harding-Cox presidential election as they came in by telephone. Announcer Leo Rosenberg stayed on air from eight in the evening until after midnight, to an audience Westinghouse itself estimated at only a few thousand listeners with home receivers.

KDKA had received the first commercial broadcasting license in the United States just days earlier. Westinghouse ran the broadcast partly to sell the radio sets it manufactured, and within two years hundreds of new stations had gone on air across the country chasing the same audience.

Nuremberg's council commissioned the globe in 1490 to show off the city's standing in geography and trade, and Martin Behaim, recently back from years in Portugal, was asked to oversee it. A painter named Georg Glockendon laid the finished map onto gores of linen stretched over a wooden and plaster core, a division of labour typical of the period, where the geographer supplied knowledge and a craftsman supplied the object.

Because the globe was finished in 1492 before word of Columbus's landfall reached Europe, it shows an open ocean between Spain and Asia with no Americas at all, a gap that makes it a snapshot of exactly what an informed European believed the world looked like the moment before that belief changed. It survives today in Nuremberg's Germanisches Nationalmuseum.

Martin Waldseemuller, a cartographer working at Saint-Die in Lorraine, printed a twelve-sheet world map in 1507 that labelled the southern continent 'America' after the Florentine explorer Amerigo Vespucci, whose published account of the South American coast had reached Europe. Waldseemuller had never met Vespucci and later dropped the name from a subsequent map, apparently unconvinced he deserved it.

The name stuck anyway, spreading through later atlases even as Waldseemuller himself wavered. Only one printed copy of the 1507 map survives, discovered in a German castle in 1901 and bought by the United States Library of Congress in 2003, which is why it is sometimes called America's birth certificate.

The Stockton and Darlington Railway opened in September 1825 to move coal from inland pits to the coast, and it is usually credited as the first public railway to carry general goods and, on that first day, passengers, using steam locomotion rather than horses over its full length. George Stephenson built the line and drove its locomotive, Locomotion No. 1, himself on the opening run.

Passenger service was at first an afterthought, carried in a horse-drawn coach called the Experiment rather than by steam, and much of the early traffic was still coal wagons. The line's success persuaded backers to fund the Liverpool and Manchester Railway five years later, which is usually credited as the first railway built for passengers from the outset.

Rome's Forum sat on marshland before the Cloaca Maxima existed. Work began around 600 BCE under Tarquinius Priscus, lining an existing stream bed with stone to carry floodwater and drainage away from the valley, and the last of the Roman kings, Tarquinius Superbus, finished the job.

It started as an open channel and was only vaulted over in stone, section by section, from the 3rd century BCE onward, centuries after the original digging. Parts of that vaulted channel still carry rainwater out of central Rome today, under streets laid long after the empire that built it.

Before any fixed code existed, a fleet's admiral simply agreed a short private list of flag meanings with his own captains before sailing, and a different admiral's list meant nothing to a stranger's ship. Early systems could send only a handful of prearranged orders, mostly about formation and attack, because there was no way to spell out an arbitrary word.

Numeral flags changed that: assign each flag a digit, and a hoist of two or three flags becomes a number that a printed signal book turns back into a sentence. English admirals refined this through the 1600s and 1700s, and the approach still underlies the international maritime flag code used by merchant ships today.

Completed in 1902 on a triangular plot where Broadway crosses Fifth Avenue, the Fuller Company's building was nicknamed for its resemblance to a cast-iron clothes iron and the name eventually replaced its formal one. At 22 storeys it was among the tallest buildings in New York at the time, though far from the tallest in the world, and its steel frame was clad in limestone and terracotta rather than masonry that carried the weight.

The narrow prow, only about two metres wide at its point, created unusual wind currents at street level that were said to lift women's skirts, drawing men to loiter nearby until police reportedly moved them along, supposedly the origin of the phrase '23 skidoo' referencing the building's address.

Florence's cathedral had stood without a roof over its crossing for decades before Brunelleschi won a 1418 competition to close the gap, a hole 45 metres wide that no one then knew how to bridge without collapsing the walls beneath it. His winning model showed a dome built in two shells, inner and outer, locked together by stone ribs rather than the wooden falsework masons assumed any dome that size would need.

Brick laid in a herringbone pattern let each course lock against the next as the curve steepened, so the structure held its own weight while still wet. Brunelleschi also designed the ox hoist that lifted materials hundreds of feet without workers descending for each load, and he is said to have kept the engineering details secret even from his own masons for fear of theft.

Before John Kay's patent in 1733, a hand loom weaver working cloth wider than his own reach needed a second person sitting opposite to catch and return the shuttle carrying the weft thread. Kay's device ran the shuttle along a track on wheels, flicked from side to side by cords a single weaver could pull, so one person could weave cloth that previously took two.

The shuttle roughly doubled how fast a weaver could work and let cloth be made wider than before, but it also meant one weaver now needed several spinners' worth of thread just to keep up, which strained the older cottage system of hand spinning. Kay made little money from the patent, weavers in Lancashire resented the job losses it implied, and he eventually left England for France.

Paired with the verge escapement, the foliot was a horizontal bar with weights slid along its arms, swinging back and forth to check the fall of the clock's driving weight and turn a continuous pull into a countable beat. Moving the weights inward or outward was the only way an early tower clock could be adjusted to run faster or slower.

It had no fixed period of its own, unlike a pendulum, so accuracy depended on trial and error by whoever tended the clock, often a paid cathedral servant rather than a specialist. The foliot survived in use for roughly three centuries before Christiaan Huygens applied the pendulum to clockwork in 1656, at which point its uneven timekeeping was quickly abandoned.

The Fuggers started as weavers in Augsburg, a trade Hans Fugger had built up from 1367. His grandson Jakob took the family into mining rather than only lending, buying rights to silver and copper deposits in the Tyrol and Hungary and controlling much of the ore Europe's mints and cannon foundries depended on by the early 1500s.

That grip on metal gave Jakob leverage banking alone could not, and in 1519 he lent Charles of Habsburg roughly 850,000 florins to buy the votes of the electors who chose the Holy Roman Emperor, securing the throne against a rival backed by French money. He died in 1525 reputedly the richest man in Europe, and the almshouses he endowed for Augsburg's poor, the Fuggerei, still house residents for the token rent he set.

In 1582 the Cossack leader Yermak Timofeyevich crossed the Ural Mountains with a few hundred men in the pay of the Stroganov merchant family and defeated the Siberian Khanate at Chuvash Cape the following year. The campaign was funded privately, not by the tsar's treasury, because the Stroganovs held a charter to exploit Siberian resources and sable pelts were worth more by weight than most metals.

Russian expansion then moved east in a chain of wooden forts, each built near a river confluence to collect fur tribute, or yasak, from local Siberian peoples. Within sixty years Russian traders had reached the Pacific coast, following the sable rather than any planned route, and the fur trade financed much of Moscow's growing state revenue along the way.

Spain's first galleon crossing between Manila and Acapulco sailed in 1565, connecting a route that Spanish silver from Mexican and Peruvian mines financed in both directions. Chinese silk, porcelain and spices moved east across the Pacific to Acapulco, and American silver moved west to Manila, where much of it was resold on into China.

One or two galleons a year made the crossing, a voyage that could take four to six months eastward against Pacific currents and cost many sailors' lives to scurvy and storms. The route ran for two and a half centuries until 1815, longer than most European trade monopolies of the era, and it was one of the first trade links to tie the Americas directly to East Asia.

Eero Saarinen won the 1947 competition to design a monument on St Louis's riverfront with a catenary arch, the shape a chain takes hanging freely, inverted. Construction did not finish until October 1965, four years after Saarinen died, leaving him another building he never saw completed. At 192 metres it is the tallest arch structure in the world.

Workers assembled it from stainless steel sections lifted by a pair of custom creeper cranes that climbed the legs as they rose, meeting at the top on 28 October 1965 with barely a centimetre of gap to spare. A tram system inside each leg still carries visitors up to an observation deck, riding through a structure that has no straight vertical anywhere along its curve.

Genoa's banking houses, families like the Spinola, Doria and Grimaldi, did not lend the way a modern bank does. Their tool was the commenda, a partnership in which an investor put up capital and a merchant sailed with it, splitting the profit of a single voyage. Bills of exchange let a debt raised in Genoa be settled in Bruges or Cairo without moving coin at all, which is what let their reach outrun their city's small size.

That reach financed both trade and war. Genoese capital backed spice cargoes from Egypt and cloth from England, and the same families extended credit to popes and kings, including the crowns fighting the Hundred Years War, at rates that made banking as profitable as the shipping it funded. The formal Bank of Saint George followed only in 1407.

Gyeongbokgung Palace in Seoul, the main royal palace of the Joseon dynasty, had lain in ruins since Japanese invasions burned it down in 1592, and no king had rebuilt it in the centuries since. The regent Heungseon Daewongun, ruling on behalf of the boy king Gojong, pushed through a reconstruction from 1865 to assert royal authority eclipsed by powerful court factions.

The Geunjeongjeon, the throne hall where the king held court and received officials, was rebuilt on its original stone terraces and finished by 1867, along with the rest of the palace complex. The project was funded by forced donations and new taxes that made it deeply unpopular, and much of what was rebuilt was destroyed again during the Japanese occupation in the early twentieth century, with restoration continuing into recent decades.

The Ghana Empire, in the western Sahel and unrelated to the modern country that later took its name, did not mine the gold it grew rich on. It controlled the trade routes where West African gold, dug further south, was exchanged for Saharan salt, taking a cut on both goods as they passed through its markets.

Arab geographers writing from the 9th century described its ruler taxing every load of salt entering the kingdom and every load of gold leaving it, a toll system rather than direct production that made Ghana wealthy on the movement of other people's goods.

The rooms are not spread evenly across a single date. Tree ring dating of the roof beams shows most of the timber was cut between 1275 and 1287, a window of roughly a dozen years rather than one building season. Forty six rooms sit across five caves above Cliff Dweller Canyon, enough for perhaps ten to fifteen families sharing the same shallow overhangs cut into volcanic rock by the Gila River.

What is unusual is how briefly the site was used. The Mogollon people who built the rooms seem to have left the caves within about twenty years, by roughly 1300, for reasons archaeologists still debate: drought, soil exhaustion, or simply that the site had served its purpose. The dry caves preserved timber, pottery and textiles that open ground rarely keeps this well.

The Globe was built in 1599 on the south bank of the Thames after the Lord Chamberlain's Men lost the lease on their previous playhouse, the Theatre, in Shoreditch. Rather than abandon the building, they dismantled its timber frame overnight and carried the wood across the frozen river to Southwark to rebuild it as the Globe.

Shakespeare held a share in the company and in the new theatre itself, an unusual arrangement that let him profit directly from performances rather than only from selling plays. The original burned down in 1613 when a cannon fired during a performance of Henry VIII set the thatched roof alight.

A gnomon is nothing more than an upright object, a post, an obelisk or later a purpose built rod, that throws a shadow whose length and direction change through the day and the year. Egyptian sundials and shadow clocks that survive from later periods, along with references in earlier texts, point to a much older habit of reading time from a shadow that the catalogue places around 3000 BCE.

Tracking where a shadow's tip fell at fixed points let Egyptians divide daylight into hours long before mechanical clocks existed, and the same shadow lengths recorded across a year mark the solstices and equinoxes. Temple alignments at sites such as Karnak show that this shadow reading was tied closely to religious calendar keeping, not treated as a separate practical craft.

The carved limestone pillars at Gobekli Tepe, in what is now south-eastern Turkey, predate pottery, writing and the wheel. They were raised by people who had not yet domesticated wheat, arranged in circles up to twenty metres across and carved with foxes, scorpions and vultures rather than any obvious deity.

No hearths, houses or middens turned up on the earliest levels, which is why archaeologists call it ceremonial rather than residential. Around 8000 BCE the builders buried the pillars under rubble on purpose, and the hill stayed sealed until excavation began in 1995, preserving carving detail a settled village would not have kept.

Chief engineer Joseph Strauss insisted on a safety net slung beneath the deck, an unusual precaution for the time that is credited with saving nineteen men who fell during construction; they called themselves the Halfway to Hell Club. Eleven other workers died on the project, ten of them in a single scaffold collapse in 1937.

The colour was never meant to be permanent. The steel arrived from the fabricator coated in a burnt orange sealant, and the consulting architect Irving Morrow chose to keep that shade, now called international orange, over the US Navy's preferred stripes of black and yellow for visibility in fog.

New Sarai, minted on Golden Horde coins as Sarai al Jadid, rose about eighty five kilometres east of modern Volgograd on a side channel of the lower Volga. It replaced an older capital, Sarai Batu, further downstream once the Horde's court and treasury shifted upstream during its wealthiest decades under Khan Uzbeg. Later chroniclers described a city of brick palaces and mosques built by captured artisans.

A near contemporary estimate, cited by Britannica, put the combined population of the two Sarai cities at around six hundred thousand, a scale that would rank either among the largest cities anywhere in the fourteenth century. The city's fortune did not last: Timur's army sacked New Sarai around 1395, and the site never fully recovered its earlier standing among the Horde's remaining strongholds.

Guru Arjan, the fifth Sikh guru, began building the Harmandir Sahib in 1585 at the centre of a sacred pool, deliberately setting entrances on all four sides so that people of any background could enter without favouring one direction over another. He completed the Adi Granth, the compiled Sikh scriptures, and installed it inside the temple in 1604.

Its gold covering came much later: Maharaja Ranjit Singh had the upper floors gilded with gold leaf in the early nineteenth century, giving the temple the appearance that earned its common English name. The site has since been rebuilt more than once after periods of destruction, including an assault by Mughal and later colonial forces.

Emperor Fasilides founded Gondar around 1636 and built the first of its stone castles there, choosing the site partly for its water and partly, tradition holds, because it fulfilled a prophecy about a place whose name began with the letter Ge. Successive emperors added their own palaces, banqueting halls, stables and churches inside the same walled enclosure over the following century.

The result, the Fasil Ghebbi compound, mixes local building traditions with forms borrowed from Portuguese Jesuit missionaries and Indian Gujarati traders who had settled at the Ethiopian court. Gondar stayed the empire's capital for roughly two hundred years before political power fragmented among regional lords, and the compound's buildings were damaged by British bombing during the Second World War before restoration work began.

Abbot Suger began rebuilding the choir of Saint-Denis in 1140, using pointed arches and ribbed vaults that carried weight down through slender piers instead of thick walls, freeing space for windows to grow. Suger wrote that he wanted light itself to feel holy, and the choir's stained glass flooded the space with coloured light on that principle.

Builders across northern France copied the formula within decades, at Chartres, Reims and Amiens among others, each pushing the vaults higher and the glass wider. The term Gothic itself came centuries later, coined as an insult by Renaissance critics who associated the style with the Goths and thought it crude.

A fire tore through Chartres in June 1194, gutting most of the church but leaving the west facade and its two towers standing. That accident let builders rebuild almost the whole cathedral in the newer Gothic style within one sustained campaign, rather than in the patched together stages seen at older churches.

Flying buttresses, still a fairly recent idea, let the nave walls rise thin and full of glass; more than 150 windows survive, including a deep cobalt long called Chartres blue, whose exact recipe glassmakers have never fully reconstructed. The rebuilt cathedral was largely complete by around 1220.

The Gotthard Base Tunnel opened in June 2016 after seventeen years of boring beneath the Swiss Alps, running 57 kilometres between Erstfeld and Bodio in two parallel single-track bores. At its deepest point the rock overhead is about 2,300 metres thick, making it the deepest railway tunnel as well as the longest.

It replaced the older Gotthard rail line's steep switchback route with a flat, level path, cutting travel time between Zurich and Milan and letting freight trains cross the Alps without the extra locomotives the old grades demanded. It forms the centrepiece of a rail link planned to run from Rotterdam to Genoa.

Grain, not cloth or spice, was the Hanseatic League's most reliable cargo. Ships loaded rye and wheat at Prussian ports along the Vistula, grown on estates worked by an unfree peasantry bound to the land specifically to keep exports flowing, and carried it west to feed cities in the Low Countries and England that could not grow enough of their own.

The League's advantage was organisation more than any single monopoly grant: member cities from Danzig to Lubeck coordinated warehousing, shipping and pricing so closely that outside merchants struggled to compete on the same routes. That grip on Baltic grain lasted for generations, only loosening as Dutch and English shippers built their own direct links to the same Prussian ports in later centuries.

Sections of canal linking China's river systems already existed, but Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty ordered them joined and extended between 604 and 609, digging new stretches such as the Tongji Canal to connect the Yellow River valley to the Yangtze and on to Hangzhou. The finished network ran well over a thousand kilometres, letting grain move by barge between north and south China instead of overland.

The project was built largely by conscripted labour under brutal conditions, and the expense helped bring down the Sui dynasty within a decade of completion. Later dynasties kept extending and repairing it, and the Grand Canal remains the longest artificial waterway still in use anywhere in the world.

The Great Belt fixed link actually splits road and rail onto different structures: a suspension bridge with the world's second-longest main span carries road traffic across the eastern channel, while trains cross the same stretch through a bored tunnel, and only the western box-girder bridge, between Zealand and Sprogo, carries both together. It replaced ferries that had linked Denmark's two largest land masses for generations.

Completed in stages through the 1990s and fully open by 1998, the crossing cut a journey that once needed an hour-long ferry down to about ten minutes by car or train. Denmark financed the whole link through tolls and state-backed loans rather than general taxation, a model since copied for the Oresund Bridge to Sweden.

Abd al-Rahman I began the mosque in 785 on the site of a former church, and successive rulers kept enlarging it for two centuries, adding rows of double-tiered horseshoe arches on reused Roman and Visigothic columns. The final expansion under al-Hakam II and his successors, finished around 987, brought the building to roughly 23,000 square metres, one of the largest mosques ever built.

After Christian forces retook Cordoba in 1236 the building became a cathedral, and in the sixteenth century a Renaissance nave was inserted directly into the middle of the forest of arches. Charles V, who authorised the change, reportedly regretted it once he saw the result, saying the builders had destroyed something unique to build something ordinary.

Workers on the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad walked out at Martinsburg, West Virginia, in July 1877 after the company cut wages for the second time that year, its earnings squeezed by a depression that had run since the Panic of 1873. The strike spread along the rail lines within days, reaching Baltimore, Pittsburgh, Chicago and St Louis without any central organisation directing it.

State militias and, eventually, federal troops sent by President Rutherford Hayes broke the strike within about six weeks, with dozens of workers killed in clashes in Pittsburgh and elsewhere. It was the first work stoppage to shut down rail traffic across much of the country, and it pushed later labour organisers toward building unions that could coordinate rather than rely on spontaneous walkouts.

China already had several regional walls before this. Around 220 BCE, Qin Shi Huang, having just unified the warring states, ordered those separate fortifications joined and extended into one continuous defensive line against raids from nomadic peoples to the north, running from Gansu in the west toward Liaodong in the east.

Almost nothing of that Qin-era wall survives; it was built largely of packed earth, and forced labour under harsh conditions killed workers in numbers no reliable count records. The stone and brick wall tourists visit near Beijing today is mostly Ming dynasty work from the 14th to 17th centuries, built more than 1,500 years later on a different line.

Builders working from around 1100 stacked granite blocks into massive walls without mortar, shaping them so precisely that the largest enclosure's curved wall still stands over 10 metres high. The site grew into the capital of a trading kingdom that dealt in gold and ivory reaching as far as China, evidenced by imported porcelain found among the ruins.

Colonial-era archaeologists, reluctant to credit an African society with the site, spent decades attributing it to Phoenicians or other outsiders despite local evidence to the contrary. That claim was abandoned once proper excavation confirmed a Bantu-speaking builders' origin, and the country later named itself after the ruins at independence in 1980.

The walls at Great Zimbabwe were laid dry, without mortar, from granite blocks split along natural fracture lines; some sections curve rather than meet at right angles and rise past six metres. A fragment of Chinese celadon pottery and imported glass beads found within the ruins mark the site as a hub feeding gold and ivory into Indian Ocean trade routes.

The kingdom's wealth is measured less by any single date than by what excavators pulled from its enclosures: cattle bones, iron gongs and eight soapstone birds, carved on tall posts, that now appear on Zimbabwe's coat of arms and currency. Its rulers controlled routes linking the interior to the Swahili coast.

Frank Gehry clad the museum in titanium panels rather than steel, a material he chose partly because it was, at the time, cheaper than expected after the price collapsed following the end of the Cold War's demand for it in aerospace. The curving forms were only feasible to build because Gehry's team used aircraft-design software, CATIA, to translate his crumpled paper models into buildable steel frames.

The museum's success in reviving a city hit hard by deindustrialisation gave the term Bilbao effect to the idea that a single striking building could revive a declining place, though later attempts elsewhere to replicate it with a landmark museum alone mostly failed. Within a few years of opening, the Guggenheim was drawing roughly a million visitors annually to a city few tourists had previously bothered to visit.

Gwadar sits on Pakistan's Arabian Sea coast, close to the Iranian border and far from any rail or major road network, which is precisely why it was chosen: a deep-water port there could bypass the long sea route around India and give landlocked western China a shorter path to open ocean. China financed and built the first phase, largely complete by 2007, well before the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor gave the port its strategic profile.

Construction proceeded slowly relative to the ambitions attached to it. Roads and a planned rail link connecting Gwadar to the rest of Pakistan lagged the port itself for years, and the surrounding town remained small and underdeveloped even as officials described the site as a future hub for regional trade.

Hadrian ordered the wall in 122 after visiting the province himself, and building took at least six years across a workforce drawn from three legions. It ran 73 miles from the Tyne to the Solway Firth, built of stone for the eastern 45 miles and turf in the west, where local stone was scarcer.

The wall was never a simple barrier: forts, milecastles and turrets every third of a mile controlled movement and collected tolls on people crossing rather than sealing the frontier shut. Rome abandoned it as a functioning boundary in the early fifth century, and much of its stone was later quarried by local builders, leaving the low, patchy ruin visible today.

The wall ran about 117 kilometres from coast to coast, built mostly by soldiers of three Roman legions rather than slave labour, with a fort or milecastle at regular intervals along its length. It never marked the true edge of Roman Britain: garrisons and roads pushed further north at times, and the wall functioned more as a controlled, taxable crossing point than a hard frontier.

Within a generation the Antonine Wall was built further north in Scotland, only to be abandoned again within about twenty years, after which Hadrian's Wall resumed its role. Large stretches survive because later builders quarried it for stone, leaving the best-preserved sections in its less accessible middle stretch.

A balance wheel on its own swings back and forth at a rate set mostly by friction and how hard it was wound, which drifts as a mainspring loses tension. Christiaan Huygens fitted a fine coiled spiral, the hairspring, to the wheel around 1675, giving it a restoring force of its own so the swing rate depended on the spring's stiffness rather than on the wound-down power feeding it.

The pairing made a pocket watch keep time closely enough to be useful rather than merely decorative, since earlier portable watches without a hairspring could lose or gain an hour or more in a day. Huygens and Hooke each claimed priority over the idea, a rerun of their earlier dispute over the pendulum clock, and the argument was never conclusively settled in either man's favour.

No single workshop or weaver can be credited with the frame loom, and the catalogue's date around 2000 BCE is a rough marker for a change visible across sites in Anatolia and the Near East rather than a recorded invention. What survives is not the wooden frames themselves, which rotted long ago, but loom weights and impressions in clay that show warp threads held taut and vertical.

A fixed frame let a weaver work faster and produce wider, more even cloth than a warp pegged to the ground or a tree. Textile fragments and the weights found at settlement sites across the region are the evidence, and similar frames appear independently in other parts of the world in the same broad period rather than spreading from one origin point.

No trace of a garden has ever turned up at Babylon, and the hundreds of surviving building inscriptions of Nebuchadnezzar II, who is credited with the gardens, never mention one. What does survive is an Assyrian relief from Nineveh showing trees on raised terraces, watered by an aqueduct the king Sennacherib boasted of building decades earlier.

That has led a number of historians to argue the wonder belongs to Sennacherib's Nineveh, roughly 550 kilometres north of Babylon, and that Greek writers, working centuries later and at second hand, simply attached the story to the wrong capital and the wrong king.

A ship's longitude could only be worked out from the difference between local time and a fixed reference time, which meant carrying an accurate clock through months at sea, when even good pendulum clocks lost minutes a day. Parliament had offered a prize of up to twenty thousand pounds for a workable solution in 1714, and the Yorkshire carpenter John Harrison spent five years building his first attempt.

Harrison's H1, finished in 1735, used counterbalanced weights and springs instead of a pendulum so it stayed accurate regardless of the ship's roll, and it was tested at sea to Lisbon the following year. He kept refining the design through three more machines over the next three decades, and it was H4, a much smaller watch, that finally satisfied the Board of Longitude's exacting trial requirements.

Herring shoal in vast numbers in the western Baltic each autumn, and by 1300 the fishing grounds off Scania, on Sweden's southern tip, drew fleets and traders from across northern Europe to seasonal fairs held at the shore. Salting the catch on site let it keep for months, turning a local glut into cargo that could reach inland markets far from any coastline.

The Hanseatic League, a federation of German trading towns led by Lubeck, controlled the salt supply that made preservation possible and took a cut of nearly every barrel traded at Scania. Herring became so central to the League's wealth that later shifts in the fish's migration, away from the Baltic in the fifteenth century, badly damaged Hanseatic finances.

The airport sits on Chek Lap Kok, an island flattened and extended with reclaimed land to make room for two parallel runways, after Hong Kong's old Kai Tak airport had become notorious for a landing approach that took jets low over apartment blocks. Building it required moving hundreds of millions of cubic metres of fill, one of the largest earthworks in Asia at the time.

Norman Foster's terminal opened in July 1998, only months before a chaotic first few days in which baggage systems and cargo handling briefly broke down under the switch from Kai Tak. Within a few years it had become one of the world's busiest airports for both passengers and air cargo, helped by a purpose-built rail and bridge link into central Hong Kong.

The Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge opened in October 2018, a 55 kilometre crossing of the Pearl River Delta made up of cable-stayed bridge sections, an undersea tunnel, and two artificial islands where the road dips beneath shipping lanes. It cut the road journey between Hong Kong and Zhuhai from about three hours to roughly thirty minutes.

At 55 kilometres it became the longest sea crossing in the world, well ahead of Louisiana's Lake Pontchartrain Causeway, which is longer overall but crosses freshwater rather than open sea. Construction spanned nine years and required reinforcing the structure against the region's typhoons.

Workers poured the concrete in interlocking columns rather than one continuous mass, because a solid block that size would have taken over a century to cool without cracking. Refrigeration pipes ran through the mix to draw the heat out artificially, and the dam still finished two years ahead of its contracted schedule in 1936.

It was called Boulder Dam for most of its construction, a compromise name after Herbert Hoover's own administration had proposed honouring him and his successor's administration objected. Congress restored the name Hoover in 1947. At 221 metres it was the tallest dam in the world when finished, a record other dams eventually surpassed.

Hopewell communities in the Ohio valley left no writing, but the materials buried in their earthwork mounds trace trade lines across most of the continent. Obsidian came from what is now Yellowstone, copper from the Great Lakes, mica from the southern Appalachians, and shells from the Gulf coast, all carried overland or by river far beyond any single group's own territory.

None of this required a state or standing merchants; goods likely passed hand to hand between neighbouring groups over long distances rather than through direct long journeys. What survives is almost entirely what was placed in burial mounds, so archaeologists are reconstructing a continent-wide network from what people chose to bury with their dead.

The Humber Bridge opened in 1981 between Hessle and Barton-upon-Humber in England, closing a gap that had forced drivers on either bank into a long detour or a ferry crossing. Its main span of 1,410 metres made it the longest single-span suspension bridge in the world, a project that had taken 24 years from parliamentary approval to opening as funding repeatedly stalled.

Like the Verrazzano-Narrows before it, the Humber's two towers had to be built slightly out of parallel, roughly 36 millimetres further apart at their tops than their bases, to account for the earth's curvature over that distance. The bridge held its world record for 16 years until Denmark's Great Belt Bridge overtook it in 1997, and it now ranks well outside the top ten.

Frankincense is dried resin tapped from Boswellia trees that grow best in the harsh, arid stretch covering southern Arabia and the Horn of Africa, a range narrow enough that supply was always limited. Burned, it produced a fragrant smoke central to temple ritual across Egypt and Mesopotamia, which meant the resin itself became a heavily traded good.

Camel caravans carried it north through the Arabian peninsula long before ships took over the route by sea. Egyptian records describe expeditions to the land the Egyptians called Punt specifically to obtain incense, and by the first millennium BCE whole cities in southern Arabia had grown wealthy on taxing the trade passing through.

On 16 April 1853 a fourteen carriage train hauled by three locomotives named Sahib, Sindh and Sultan carried around 400 passengers roughly 21 miles from Bori Bunder in Bombay to Thane. The Great Indian Peninsula Railway had built the line, and colonial officials treated the opening as a showpiece of British engineering brought to the subcontinent.

Governor General Lord Dalhousie had pushed hard for Indian railways as tools of trade and troop movement, and this first short line grew within decades into one of the largest rail networks in the world. It also created a new kind of workforce, since running steam railways at this scale required training thousands of Indian engineers, drivers and clerks almost from nothing.

Woad, extracted from a European plant, gave a weaker, muddier blue than indigo pressed from the leaves of Indigofera grown in Gujarat and Bengal. Once Portuguese ships began carrying Indian indigo cakes home in bulk, dyers in Flanders and England could get a stronger colour at a lower cost per garment than they could from local woad fields.

Woad growers lobbied hard against the newcomer, and several German states banned indigo import in the sixteenth century on the grounds that it was a corrosive fraud rather than a true dye. The bans did not hold. By the following century indigo had displaced woad across most of the European cloth trade, and woad farming survived only in scattered pockets.

Assembly began on 20 November 1998 when a Russian Proton rocket launched the Zarya control module, funded and built by Russia but paid for by NASA, an arrangement born out of Cold War rivals suddenly needing each other's hardware. The American Unity module joined it two weeks later, launched on the Space Shuttle Endeavour and bolted on by astronauts during a spacewalk.

What began as two modules grew over more than a decade into a structure the length of a football pitch, assembled from pieces built in the United States, Russia, Europe, Japan and Canada and launched on rockets and shuttles from three different countries. It has been continuously occupied since November 2000, longer than any spacecraft before it.

Eisenhower had driven with a military convoy across the country in 1919, a trip that took over two months on roads that kept breaking trucks and axles, and later saw Germany's autobahns during the war. Both experiences fed into the case for a national highway network he pushed through Congress with the Federal Aid Highway Act of 1956.

The act paid 90 percent of construction costs from a new highway trust fund financed by fuel taxes, an arrangement that let states build far faster than they could alone. The network eventually ran to over 40,000 miles, reshaping American commuting, freight and the layout of cities it bypassed.

Cast by Abraham Darby III at his family's Coalbrookdale ironworks and designed with the architect Thomas Pritchard, the bridge opened to traffic on 1 January 1781, spanning the Severn gorge with roughly 378 tons of iron in a single arch over 100 feet across. It let barge traffic pass beneath uninterrupted, something a timber or stone bridge of that span could not have managed.

Its joints copied carpentry techniques, dovetails and wedges, because nobody had cast a structure this large before and iron bridge design had no precedent to follow. The bridge nearly bankrupted the Darby family despite its engineering success, and the small riverside settlement that grew up around it took the bridge's own name, becoming the town of Ironbridge.

Masons had tied stone with metal for centuries, but Renaissance builders widened its use, setting iron rods and clamps inside chains of masonry to resist the outward thrust of a wide dome or vault rather than just pinning blocks together at a joint. Michelangelo specified an iron chain around the drum of St Peter's dome in Rome to counter exactly this kind of spreading force.

The iron was set into channels cut in the stone and packed with molten lead or mortar, which let it flex slightly with temperature rather than crack the masonry around it. Rusting iron eventually became the failure it was meant to prevent in some buildings, since expanding corrosion could split the very stone it was meant to hold together, a problem later engineers solved only by better sealing and, eventually, other metals.

The Grand Bazaar runs from the Naqsh-e Jahan square in a single vaulted corridor to the older Jameh Mosque, a route that let Shah Abbas fold a marketplace already centuries old into his new capital rather than start one from scratch. Brick domes lit by small round openings kept the corridor shaded and ventilated through Isfahan's hot summers, a design copied in bazaars across Iran afterward.

Its stalls were sorted by trade, so a buyer could walk from the coppersmiths' section to the carpet sellers' without doubling back, a layout still recognisable today. Caravanserais along its length housed merchants overnight, and the bazaar's income from rents and tolls helped fund the mosques and bridges Abbas built elsewhere in the city.

Shah Abbas I did not build a new city so much as rebuild an old one around a new open square, the Naqsh-e Jahan, large enough that polo matches were staged on it. The goalposts still stand at either end, a detail that tells visitors the space was meant for use, not just for looking at.

Isfahan's bridges over the Zayandeh River carried water as well as traffic: the Khaju bridge doubled as a dam with sluice gates, and its arched terraces were built for people to sit in during floods. The move of the capital from Qazvin pulled merchants and craftsmen with it, and Persian carpets and silk sold there reached European buyers within Abbas's own reign.

Nebuchadnezzar II built the Ishtar Gate around 575 BCE as one of eight gates through Babylon's inner walls, facing the processional way used for the New Year festival. Its surface of blue-glazed bricks, moulded into rows of striding lions, bulls and mythical dragons called sirrush, was made by firing glazed tiles individually and assembling them like a relief puzzle.

German archaeologist Robert Koldewey excavated the gate's foundations between 1902 and 1914, and its bricks were shipped to Berlin, where a reconstructed version stands in the Pergamon Museum today. The original site in Iraq now holds only the buried lower courses and a smaller replica built under Saddam Hussein.

Sultan Ahmed I ordered the mosque after a run of military losses against Persia and Austria, an unusual motive for a building meant to restore his standing rather than mark a victory. Its six minarets caused a stir at the time because only the mosque in Mecca had that many, and legend holds the sultan's architect misheard a request for gold minarets as a request for six.

Its familiar name comes from more than 20,000 handmade Iznik tiles lining the upper walls and dome, mostly blue and turquoise floral patterns lit by 260 windows. Ahmed did not live to see it long: he died the year after it was completed, and he is buried in a tomb built into its outer courtyard.

Itaipu straddles the Parana River between Brazil and Paraguay, and the two countries split its output evenly by treaty even though Paraguay uses only a fraction of its half, selling the rest to its larger neighbour. Concrete poured for the project would have built five copies of the Itaipu stadium in Rio, and the diverted river channel used during construction ranks among the largest earth-moving efforts on record.

China's Three Gorges Dam overtook Itaipu's installed capacity in the 2000s, but Itaipu still holds the record for total electricity generated in a single year, a title it has traded back and forth with Three Gorges since 2016 depending on rainfall. In some years it alone has supplied around ninety per cent of Paraguay's electricity and a sixth of Brazil's.

Ground was broken in April 2013 on a tower designed to clear 1,008 metres, well past the Burj Khalifa's 828, and become the first building over a kilometre tall. The contractor, Saudi Binladin Group, was caught up in a 2017 corruption purge, and work stalled the following January with the tower stuck at 63 floors.

It sat unfinished for roughly seven years before a new completion contract restarted work in late 2024, aiming for 2028. Its site, Jeddah's northern shore on the Red Sea, was picked so the tower would eventually anchor an entire planned district around it, not just a skyline.

Cherry trees had to be moved to clear the site, and the women who had campaigned to plant them chained themselves to the trees in protest before the government relented and replanted many elsewhere on the Tidal Basin. The memorial's circular, domed design deliberately echoed Jefferson's own home at Monticello and the Pantheon he admired.

The bronze statue at its centre was cast in plaster for the 1943 dedication because wartime metal restrictions made bronze unavailable; the actual bronze figure was not installed until 1947. Franklin Roosevelt, who championed the memorial, attended the dedication on Jefferson's two hundredth birthday.

Djenne sits on the floodplain of the Bani River, and that seasonal flooding is what made it valuable: goods could be moved by boat much of the year, and the city grew from around the 9th century into a market where gold and salt from further afield changed hands, alongside people sold into slavery along the same routes.

The city's mudbrick Great Mosque, rebuilt repeatedly on the same site since a first structure went up in the 13th century, is resurfaced with fresh mud by the community every year after the rainy season, a maintenance ritual that keeps a building this old still standing at all.

Long before the biblical trumpets, Jericho's inhabitants raised a stone wall over four metres high and a tower nearly nine metres tall beside a freshwater spring. Excavations by Kathleen Kenyon in the 1950s dated this construction to roughly 8000 BCE, thousands of years before the settlement had any writing or pottery.

Archaeologists still argue over what the wall was for. It could have kept out raiders drawn by the spring and stored grain, but its position also matches the path of flash floods off the nearby Judean hills, so some read it as flood defence that only later hardened into a fortification.

Daniel Libeskind's design has no obvious front door. Visitors enter through a neighbouring baroque building and descend into the zigzag structure through underground passages that cross at odd angles, one leading to a garden of tilted concrete columns, another dead-ending in a bare concrete tower called the Holocaust Void that is left unheated and largely unlit.

The building opened to the public in 2001, two years after construction finished, because it stood empty while curators decided what exhibition could match a structure that was already being read as a monument in its own right. Thin diagonal window slits, cut without a fixed pattern, are widely read as tracing lines between addresses once occupied by Berlin's Jewish community on a prewar map.

Chicago's John Hancock Center topped out in 1969 with a tapered black form and diagonal steel X-braces running up its exterior, a structural system engineer Fazlur Rahman Khan devised to let the tower resist wind without a bulky internal frame. The bracing let the tapered tower stack apartments, offices, parking and an observation deck in one building rather than several.

Khan's trussed-tube approach, first proven at scale here, cut the amount of steel needed compared with conventional skyscraper frames of the era and influenced tall buildings that followed it, including his own later Sears Tower. At 344 metres including its antennae, the Hancock was Chicago's second-tallest building at completion and remains one of the few towers where the structure's bracing is also its exterior decoration.

The West Baray at Angkor is a rectangular reservoir roughly eight kilometres long, dug largely by hand around 1100 to hold monsoon runoff through the dry season. Sediment cores taken from its bed show layers of silt built up gradually over generations of use, rather than a single dated feat of engineering.

Canals fed from the barays irrigated rice fields that historians think supported a population in the hundreds of thousands around Angkor. Those same canals silted over time and struggled with erratic rainfall in later centuries, and faltering water management is now counted among the pressures behind Angkor's decline after 1400.

Bayon, raised under Jayavarman VII after 1181, sets it apart from Angkor Wat: its towers carry 216 carved faces, smiling faintly, that most scholars read as the king merged with the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara rather than as straightforward portraits of Jayavarman.

Angkor Wat's temple mountain form, a central tower ringed by galleries representing Mount Meru, reached its clearest expression around 1150 and was varied afterward at Bayon, Ta Prohm and dozens of smaller sites, each raised by a different king asserting the same claim to cosmic order over the Khmer realm.

The Khwarezmian oasis depended on canals drawn off the Amu Darya, engineered so meltwater flowing down from the Pamirs each spring could be routed onto fields in a region that otherwise sees almost no rain. Archaeologists have traced canal networks near the old capital, Konye-Urgench, dating well before 1200 and repeatedly rebuilt over generations.

That irrigation supported cities wealthy enough to briefly rival larger Central Asian powers, until the Mongol invasion of 1220 breached dams and diverted the river as a weapon of war. Chroniclers writing afterward describe fields ruined for generations, long after the armies that broke the canals had moved on.

Portuguese visitors in the sixteenth century compared Mbanza Kongo's size favourably to Lisbon, and church records from the 1620s, counting baptisms performed in the city and its immediate surroundings, are consistent with a population in the tens of thousands living on the mountain itself and well over 100,000 across the wider settlement it anchored.

The city had been the kingdom's seat since around 1390, long before any European reached it, and it took the Portuguese name Sao Salvador after King Afonso I built a cathedral there in the early 1500s. It kept that dual identity, an African capital under a Portuguese saint's name, until the kingdom's power finally broke apart under civil war and slave raiding in the following two centuries.

Diogo Cao was searching for a route around Africa to India when his ships reached the mouth of the Congo river in 1483. He left a stone pillar, a padrao, marking the landfall for the Portuguese crown, then travelled upriver far enough to make contact with officials of the Kongo Kingdom before sailing on to explore further south.

The kingdom's ruler, Nzinga a Nkuwu, sent envoys back to Lisbon with Cao's returning ships, and within a decade he was baptised as a Christian under the name Joao. His son Afonso I went further, adopting Portuguese titles and court customs while keeping the kingdom's own political structure intact, a relationship that stayed relatively equal for a generation before the slave trade reshaped it.

The Kowoj Maya settled around Lake Peten Itza in what is now northern Guatemala well after the great Classic Maya cities to the north had emptied out. Their lakeside towns belong to the Postclassic period, when Maya political life had shifted away from the monumental temple centres toward smaller, fortified settlements built for defence as much as ceremony.

Sites like Zacpeten sat on peninsulas jutting into the lake, an arrangement that limited access on the landward side and made the water itself part of the defences. Kowoj communities in this region survived, still practising traditional Maya religion, until Spanish forces finally conquered the last independent Maya kingdom there in 1697.

Ivan III hired Italian engineers, familiar with the fortifications of Milan, to rebuild Moscow's wooden citadel in brick between 1485 and 1495. Their triangular circuit of walls and 20 towers borrowed Italian military engineering while housing distinctly Russian cathedrals and palaces inside.

The walls were not always red: for a period under Catherine the Great they were whitewashed, and the deep red now associated with the Kremlin became fixed only after later restorations. Its towers acquired the ruby stars now on top only in the Soviet era, replacing the double-headed eagles that had marked imperial rule.

Los Angeles City Hall opened in 1928 at 452 feet, tall only because it was exempted from a 1904 municipal ordinance capping other buildings at 150 feet. That rule, meant to keep the city from crowding its streets with skyscrapers, effectively guaranteed City Hall's tower would dominate the skyline by law rather than by engineering ambition.

The height cap was repealed in 1957 once earthquake engineering and fire codes had advanced enough to make tall buildings safer, but City Hall was not actually overtaken until 1966, when the Union Bank building opened downtown. Its silhouette had already become a fixture of Los Angeles's image, appearing on the LAPD badge and in countless films before it lost its record.

Peter the Great ordered the canal in 1718 to give barges a way around Lake Ladoga, whose storms had wrecked hundreds of cargo vessels trying to reach the new capital at St Petersburg. Construction began in 1719 and the channel, linking the Neva and Volkhov rivers along the lake's southern shore, was finished in 1730, five years after Peter's death.

It was one of the largest hydraulic engineering projects attempted anywhere in Europe that century, dug largely by hand and forced labour over more than a decade. The canal kept goods bound for St Petersburg off the open lake entirely, and it stayed in active use until a second, deeper Ladoga canal was built alongside it in the 1860s.

Louisiana finished a second, parallel span of the Lake Pontchartrain Causeway in 1969, running alongside the original 1956 bridge to handle growing traffic between New Orleans and its northern suburbs. The new span was only about 15 metres longer than the first, but the pairing gave the crossing a combined length of nearly 38.4 kilometres, most of it with no land in sight in either direction.

Guinness World Records recognised the causeway as the longest bridge over continuous water on its completion, a title it held unchallenged for decades. China's Jiaozhou Bay Bridge opened in 2011 and Guinness split the category rather than hand over one title outright: Jiaozhou Bay took longest bridge over water overall, while the Louisiana causeway kept the record for the longest bridge over continuous water.

Almost all lapis lazuli used in the ancient Near East came from one place: the Sar-e-Sang mines in the Badakhshan mountains of what is now Afghanistan. Nowhere else was known to produce the deep blue stone in quantity, which made every piece found in an Egyptian or Mesopotamian tomb evidence of a very long supply chain.

Tutankhamun's burial mask uses lapis for the eyebrows and eyeliner around eyes rimmed with the stone, brought west over well over a thousand miles of mountain and desert. Sumerian cities such as Ur were trading it by the mid third millennium BCE, valuing it enough to bury it with their dead alongside gold.

Lapita sites are identified by one thing above all: pottery stamped with fine geometric patterns using a toothed tool, found scattered from the Bismarck Archipelago east to Fiji, Tonga and Samoa. Dates on the earliest sherds run to roughly 1500 BCE, marking a rapid spread across thousands of kilometres of open Pacific water.

The people who made this pottery were the first humans to reach many of these islands, carrying pigs, chickens and root crops in outrigger canoes. Their language is reconstructed as an early branch of the Austronesian family, ancestral to the Polynesian languages later spoken across the wider Pacific.

Construction of Pisa's bell tower began in 1173 on ground too soft and uneven to support its weight evenly, and the tilt appeared before builders had even finished the third storey. Work then stopped for nearly a century because of wars, an accidental pause that let the unstable soil settle and probably kept the tower from toppling outright.

Engineers compensated for the lean by angling later storeys back toward vertical, giving the finished tower a slight banana curve rather than a straight slant. A twentieth century campaign of soil removal on the raised side reduced the tilt and stabilised the structure, work completed in 2001 after the tower had been closed to visitors for over a decade.

Ole Kirk Christiansen's small Danish carpentry firm had already been making wooden toys and plastic bricks for a decade when his son Godtfred filed the patent for the improved stud and tube coupling system in 1958. Earlier Lego bricks, and a similar British brick called Kiddicraft, could not grip each other securely enough to build tall or stable structures.

The new tube design let bricks clutch together firmly while still pulling apart by hand, and that geometry has stayed essentially unchanged since. A brick moulded in 1958 still fits one bought new today, a compatibility the company has protected through repeated patent and trademark disputes over the decades.

A letter of exchange let a merchant in Florence pay a debt in Bruges without moving a single coin: he handed over cash or credit locally, and a partner bank honoured the equivalent sum abroad in a different currency, on a set future date. The arrangement doubled as a way around church bans on charging interest, since the fee was folded into the exchange rate rather than named as a loan.

Family banking houses such as the Bardi and Peruzzi of Florence built branch networks across France, England and the papal court specifically to make these instruments work, since honouring a letter required a partner already present in the receiving city. Their later collapses, tied to loans made to the English crown, showed how far that credit web had come to depend on a single risky borrower.

Elizabeth I granted the Levant Company its charter in 1581, giving a group of London merchants a monopoly on English trade with the Ottoman Empire in exchange for a share of profits and diplomatic usefulness abroad. The company effectively took over English ambassadorial costs in Constantinople, since the crown had little spare money for embassies of its own.

English ships brought back currants, silk and cotton from Ottoman ports, and the company's Constantinople trading post doubled as an unofficial embassy for decades. Some of the same merchants later helped fund the East India Company, formed in 1600, using contacts and capital built up through Levant Company trade.

Lever Brothers built its Park Avenue headquarters as an advertisement for cleanliness itself. The tower's glass and steel skin, hung on a frame rather than walls that carried weight, could be washed by a mechanical rig running on tracks along its face, a novelty at the time meant to keep the soap company's own building visibly spotless.

Designed by Gordon Bunshaft at Skidmore, Owings and Merrill and finished in 1952, it raised its slab off the ground on stilts and left most of the site as open plaza, breaking from the solid masonry towers that had defined Park Avenue. Other architects copied the glass curtain wall for office towers across American cities through the following decade.

Thomas Edison did not invent the light bulb; incandescent lamps using platinum or carbon filaments had already been demonstrated by several inventors over the previous decades. What Edison's Menlo Park laboratory achieved in October 1879 was a carbonised filament, eventually cotton thread and later bamboo, that burned in a vacuum long enough and cheaply enough to be commercially viable.

Edison also built the surrounding system that made the bulb useful: generators, wiring, meters and sockets, patented and marketed together. His Pearl Street power station in lower Manhattan began supplying electric light to paying customers in 1882, turning the bulb from a laboratory curiosity into household infrastructure.

Ptolemy I began the lighthouse on the island of Pharos around 290 BCE, and it was finished under his son Ptolemy II close to 280 BCE. Ancient estimates put it above 100 metres tall, built in tapering stone stages, square base then octagonal then round, with a fire kept burning at the top and, according to later accounts, a mirror arrangement that could reflect sunlight far out to sea.

The lighthouse survived largely intact for well over a thousand years, longer than any of the other ancient Wonders, before a series of earthquakes between the tenth and fourteenth centuries brought it down in stages. Its remaining blocks were reused in the 1480s to build the fort that still occupies the site, Qaitbay Citadel, in modern Alexandria.

The memorial opened in May 1922 on reclaimed marshland along the Potomac, its site chosen only after decades of argument over whether a memorial to Lincoln should be a grand building at all or something plainer. Architect Henry Bacon modelled it on a Greek temple, with 36 columns representing the states of the Union at the time of Lincoln's death.

Sculptor Daniel Chester French's seated statue inside was carved from 28 blocks of Georgia marble, assembled so precisely that the joins are barely visible. The memorial's steps became a stage for civil rights history it was never designed for, most famously when Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his 'I Have a Dream' speech there in 1963.

The Lion Gate, built into Mycenae's citadel wall around 1250 BCE, is named for the relief above its lintel showing two lionesses flanking a central column, carved on a triangular limestone slab that lightens the load on the doorway beneath. It is the only large-scale sculpture known to survive from Mycenaean Greece.

The gate's lintel stone is estimated to weigh around twenty tonnes, set between jambs of similarly massive blocks. By the time classical Greeks visited the ruins centuries later, they no longer knew who had built it, which is part of why Cyclopean masonry, work credited to mythical giants, became the term for construction on this scale.

The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened in September 1830, built from the outset to run scheduled steam locomotives hauling both goods and paying passengers on double track between two major cities. Unlike the earlier Stockton and Darlington line, it never relied on horse traction for its passenger service, which is why historians usually credit it as the first true modern railway.

Its opening day was marred when the MP William Huskisson was struck and killed by Stephenson's Rocket while crossing the tracks to greet the Duke of Wellington, an early and widely reported demonstration of how fast the new locomotives actually moved. Despite the accident, the line proved so profitable that it set the template investors used to fund railways across Britain over the following decade.

Richard Rogers put the lifts, ductwork and staircases on the outside in steel and glass towers so the interior could stay open around a vast atrium, a decision that let the insurance market's trading floor keep its historic underwriting Room intact at the centre. Critics nicknamed it the inside-out building before most had set foot inside.

It became a Grade I listed building in 2011, the youngest structure ever given that protection in Britain, only twenty-five years after it opened. Listing normally follows decades of settled reputation, so Historic England's decision effectively fast-tracked a building whose services were, by design, meant to be replaced and repaired in view.

It was meant to be temporary. The wheel's five-year planning permission was tied to the millennium, and its designers, husband-and-wife architects David Marks and Julia Barfield, expected it to come down long before it became one of London's most photographed structures. It opened to the public on 9 March 2000, a few months late for the millennium itself, after the final capsules were fitted while the wheel was already turning.

At 135 metres it was the tallest observation wheel in the world when it opened, a title it held until the Star of Nanchang overtook it in 2006. Each of its 32 sealed glass capsules represents one of London's boroughs, and a full rotation takes about thirty minutes, slow enough that the wheel rarely stops to let passengers on.

The Metropolitan Railway opened in January 1863 between Paddington and Farringdon, built by the cut and cover method: dig a trench along the street, brick over it, then put the road back on top. Steam locomotives hauled the carriages, and smoke was meant to vent through gaps along the route, though passengers still complained about the choking air underground.

Around 38,000 people rode it on the opening day alone, showing there was real demand for a way to cross central London without fighting horse-drawn traffic on the surface. Electric traction did not arrive until the 1890s, decades after this first line proved the idea could work, and it remained smoky, steam-hauled and gas-lit for its first three decades.

President Francois Mitterrand chose I.M. Pei, a Chinese American architect with no previous major work in France, to redesign the entrance to a museum that traces its walls back to a twelfth century fortress. Parisians who objected to a glass pyramid beside a Renaissance palace called the scheme an act of vandalism before it was even built.

The structure is built from 673 glass panes rather than the often-repeated 666, a myth that stuck partly because of its satanic overtones. Beneath the glass, Pei's design solved a practical problem: it let daylight into a new subterranean lobby that could funnel far larger crowds into the museum's three wings than the old entrances ever could.

Machu Picchu sits on a ridge between two peaks at 2,430 metres, chosen with enough precision that its main buildings align to the sunrise at the June solstice. The estate is thought to have housed perhaps 750 people at most, mainly nobles, priests and the retainers who served Pachacuti's court on visits away from Cusco, rather than a large working population.

Its stonework fits without mortar, blocks cut and ground until their faces met closely enough to withstand Andean earthquakes by flexing slightly rather than cracking. The Inca abandoned the site within a century, and Spanish forces never recorded finding it, which is why it survived largely unlooted until Hiram Bingham was guided there by local farmers in 1911.

Before synthetic dyes, red cloth meant madder. The plant's root, dried and ground to a powder, was the main source of durable red and pink dye available to European weavers, and it grew especially well in the sandy soils of Zeeland and other parts of the Low Countries, which built a trade advantage around a crop that other regions could not match as cheaply.

Growing madder was slow and labour heavy: roots needed two or three years in the ground before harvest, then drying and grinding before a dyer could use them. That long cycle, combined with the Low Countries' near lock on supply, kept prices high and made madder merchants wealthy without any single ruler needing to grant a formal monopoly charter over the trade.

Malacca had no gold, spice or silk of its own. Its advantage was the strait it sat beside, the narrowest passage between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea, where monsoon winds reversed direction every six months and forced ships from both directions to wait in the same harbour. A Malay ruler named Parameswara founded the port around 1400 and its sultans built wealth by taxing that wait rather than producing anything to sell.

By the 1430s the port kept officials called shahbandars, each responsible for one foreign community, such as Gujarati or Chinese traders, managing customs and settling disputes within that group. That system let merchants speaking dozens of languages settle differences without one common law, a large part of why Malacca held its position until the Portuguese seized it in 1511.

Sultan Hasan's mosque and madrasa complex, raised in Cairo between 1356 and 1363, gives a sense of the scale Mamluk patrons reached for: about a hundred and fifty metres long, with an eastern minaret rising to sixty four metres, and four separate madrasas opening off its central courtyard, one for each Sunni school of law. Hasan himself was murdered before the building was finished.

That pattern, a sultan commissioning a mosque, teaching college and his own tomb as one structure, repeated across Cairo for the next century and a half under Barquq, Qaytbay and others. The buildings doubled as legitimacy: erecting a monumental waqf, an endowed charitable foundation, was how a Mamluk sultan, typically a former slave soldier with no hereditary claim, wrote his name permanently into the city he ruled.

The resort's three curved towers lean outward at an angle steep enough that engineers built and tested a full-scale mockup of the connection before trusting the design, then linked the towers at the top with a single 340-metre platform holding the rooftop pool, longer than the Eiffel Tower laid on its side. It opened in stages through 2010, with the casino and hotel rooms operating months before the SkyPark and its pool were finished.

Architect Moshe Safdie designed the platform to read as a ship balanced across three hulls, a form chosen partly so the resort's silhouette would be identifiable from across the bay. The infinity pool sits 57 storeys up and became one of the most photographed swimming pools in the world within its first year open.

Architect Bertrand Goldberg designed Marina City to keep Chicagoans from fleeing to the suburbs, packing apartments, a theatre, a bowling alley, a marina and parking into two round concrete towers finished in 1964. The scalloped balconies gave each unit curved outdoor space instead of a flat ledge, and for a few years the towers were the tallest concrete structures and the tallest residential buildings in the world.

The lower third of each tower is an open-air parking ramp, the wedge-shaped floors visible from outside as the corn cob's husk. Goldberg had trained under Mies van der Rohe but rejected the glass box entirely, arguing that Chicago needed round forms and mixed uses rather than another rectangular slab, and the towers still function largely as he planned them, apartments above cars above a marina.

The Medici Bank ran on a structure that kept its owners at arm's length from ruin: each branch, from Rome to Bruges to London, was a separate partnership under a local manager, so one branch's bad debts could not by themselves pull down the whole house.
