Bernini's bronze baldachin over the altar, raised on twisting columns, was not added until years after the consecration, a reminder that completion dates like 1626 mark a milestone inside a longer project rather than a true end.

The statue was dedicated on 28 October 1886, a gift from France meant to mark a century of American independence, though it arrived ten years late because both countries struggled to fund their halves of the project. Frenchman Joseph Pulitzer used his newspaper to raise the final money for the pedestal from ordinary readers after wealthier donors balked at the cost.

Sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi built the copper skin over an iron framework designed by Gustave Eiffel, whose lattice tower would rise in Paris three years later. The torch has been closed to the public since a 1916 explosion at a nearby munitions depot damaged the arm, and visitors have not been allowed up it since.

The Statue of Unity was unveiled on 31 October 2018 on Sadhu Bet island in Gujarat, on what would have been Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel's birthday. Patel was India's first deputy prime minister and the figure credited with persuading hundreds of princely states to join the Indian union after independence, the unity the statue's name refers to.

At 182 metres it passed China's Spring Temple Buddha to become the tallest statue in the world, nearly twice the height of the Statue of Liberty including its pedestal. It took about three years to build and reportedly cost over four hundred million dollars, funded partly by melting down farmers' donated iron tools.

James Watt did not invent the steam engine; Thomas Newcomen had built working ones decades earlier for pumping water out of mines. Watt's 1769 patent added a separate condenser, so the cylinder no longer had to be cooled and reheated on every stroke, cutting fuel use dramatically and making steam power practical well beyond mine sites for the first time.

Watt reached the idea while repairing a model Newcomen engine at Glasgow University and spent years afterward refining it with the manufacturer Matthew Boulton, who financed the venture. Their engines went on to drive cotton mills, ironworks and eventually locomotives, giving factories a power source that no longer depended on a river or a windy hillside.

Before Djoser's tomb at Saqqara, Egyptian royal burials were low rectangular mounds of mud brick called mastabas. His architect, Imhotep, stacked six mastabas of decreasing size on top of each other in cut limestone, producing a stepped tower roughly sixty metres tall around 2650 BCE, the first building of its scale made almost entirely of stone.

Imhotep is one of the few named architects to survive from ancient Egypt at all; later inscriptions credit him and, centuries afterward, Egyptians worshipped him as a god of medicine and wisdom. The step pyramid's surrounding complex, walled courtyards and dummy buildings, still stands beneath the sand at Saqqara today.

William Ged was an Edinburgh goldsmith with no background in printing when he worked out a way to cast a whole page of set type as a single solid plate, rather than keeping thousands of individual metal letters locked in a frame for every reprint. He patented the process in 1725, and by around 1727 he had produced working plates, though Edinburgh's printers refused to touch it, fearing it would put type founders out of work.

A partnership in London in 1729 went no better, undone by uncooperative workmen and partners Ged later blamed for sabotage, and he died in 1749 largely unrewarded. Stereotyping was revived and improved in the early nineteenth century using plaster and papier mache moulds, and it became standard for cheap mass printing of books and newspapers long after Ged's own attempts had failed.

By around 2500 BCE the sarsen stones at Stonehenge, some weighing over twenty tonnes, had been dragged roughly thirty kilometres from the Marlborough Downs and raised into the trilithon arrangement still visible today. The smaller bluestones inside the ring came from much further, a set of Welsh hills over 200 kilometres away, a haulage distance that still has no settled explanation.

The stones were shaped with mortice and tenon joints borrowed from woodworking, locking lintels onto their uprights rather than simply balancing them. Excavated cremated remains, dating across several centuries around this period, show the site kept being used as a burial ground even as its stone architecture was still being finished.

The first phase at Stonehenge was not a ring of tall stones but a circular ditch and bank enclosing a ring of pits, later known as the Aubrey Holes, dug into Salisbury Plain around 3000 BCE. Some pits held cremated human remains, making the site a cemetery centuries before the sarsens most visitors recognise were ever moved into place.

The famous upright stones came much later, raised in stages from around 2500 BCE. That gap of roughly five hundred years between the ditch and the stone circle is easy to miss when the monument is treated as a single construction rather than a project reworked by generations who never met its first builders.

The canal opened on 17 November 1869 after ten years of digging by a workforce that at times relied on forced Egyptian labour, a practice the project's financier, Ferdinand de Lesseps, only phased out after European objections and the introduction of steam dredgers. It let ships sail between Europe and Asia without rounding Africa, cutting thousands of miles from the route.

Egypt's ruler had bought a large stake in the venture to help finance it, but mounting debt forced the sale of Egypt's shares to Britain in 1875. That purchase gave Britain a controlling interest in the waterway and helped draw the country into occupying Egypt seven years later.

On 9 May 1980 the freighter Summit Venture, blinded by a squall, struck a support column of the old Sunshine Skyway and dropped a 396 metre section of roadway into Tampa Bay, killing thirty-five people, most of them in a bus and cars that drove straight off the broken edge. The replacement opened in 1987 as a cable-stayed span built to survive exactly that kind of impact.

Its single tower and yellow cables were designed with reinforced dolphin piers, artificial islands meant to stop a ship before it ever reaches the bridge deck. The new Skyway also carries a fixed span roughly 15 metres higher than its predecessor, giving large vessels far more clearance as they pass beneath.

The stone in Swahili stone towns is coral, cut from the reef and fossil coral beds along the coast and set with lime mortar, a building material found almost nowhere else this consistently in medieval sub-Saharan Africa. Kilwa, Mombasa and other city-states along the coast of what is now Tanzania and Kenya used it for mosques, palaces and merchant houses, distinct from the timber and thatch that most of their inland trading partners built with.

These towns sat on the Indian Ocean trade network, exchanging gold, ivory and enslaved people from the interior for cloth, porcelain and glass carried by Arab, Persian and later Chinese and Indian ships. Kilwa's Great Mosque, expanded repeatedly, and its ruler's Husuni Kubwa palace stand among the largest stone structures anywhere on the coast before European contact.

Norman Foster's tower at 30 St Mary Axe has a diagrid steel frame wrapped in a spiralling pattern of glass, a curved profile chosen to reduce wind loading on the ground and let air circulate up through gaps in the floor plates instead of relying purely on mechanical ventilation. Londoners nicknamed it the Gherkin almost as soon as construction topped out, and the name displaced the developer's own branding within its first year.

It opened in 2003 on the site of the Baltic Exchange, which had been badly damaged by an IRA bomb in 1992, and became the City of London's first tall building designed explicitly around energy efficiency rather than maximum floor area. It was sold in 2007 for a sum that, at the time, made it Britain's most expensive office building.

A man on a horse rode across the deck before the ribbon was cut. Francis de Groot, a member of a right wing paramilitary group opposed to the state premier, slashed the ceremonial ribbon with his sword ahead of the official opening on 19 March 1932, delaying the real ceremony by minutes and making the front pages instead of the bridge itself.

The single steel arch, built to carry trains, trams and cars between the city and the north shore, was for decades the widest long span bridge in the world by deck width. It held that particular distinction until wider road decks elsewhere overtook it. Sixteen men died during its eight years of construction, mostly from falls.

Danish architect Jorn Utzon won the 1957 design competition with sketches so rough that some judges initially rejected them before senior judge Eero Saarinen insisted on a second look. Work on the podium began in 1959 before Utzon had actually solved how to build the shell shaped roofs he had drawn, a gap that stalled the site for years.

The solution, arrived at only after 1961, was to base every shell on sections of a single sphere so the curved concrete ribs could be precast rather than individually moulded. Cost overruns and political pressure eventually drove Utzon to resign in 1966, years before the building opened, and he never returned to see it finished.

Danish architect Jorn Utzon won the 1957 design competition with sketches of sail-like shells, but nobody, including Utzon, yet knew how to build them. Engineers spent years searching for a workable geometry before realising that every shell could be carved from sections of the same imaginary sphere, letting them be cast from standardised moulds rather than shaped individually.

Utzon resigned in 1966 amid disputes over cost and design control with the New South Wales government and never saw the building finished or, for decades, set foot in it again. The project's budget grew from an original estimate of about 7 million Australian dollars to roughly 102 million by the time it opened in October 1973, largely funded through a dedicated lottery rather than general taxation.

Taipei sits in an earthquake zone prone to typhoons, so the tower's engineers hung a 660-tonne steel pendulum, visible through windows near the top, to counteract sway from wind and tremors. The building's 101 storeys are grouped visually into eight repeating sections of eight floors each, a number chosen for its associations with prosperity in Chinese culture rather than for structural reasons.

It opened on 31 December 2004 at 508 metres and was immediately the tallest building in the world, a title it held for just over five years. The Burj Khalifa overtook it in January 2010, though Taipei 101's damper and record-setting elevators, which travelled at up to 60 kilometres per hour, kept it a reference point for supertall design well after it lost the height record.

Shah Jahan began the Taj Mahal in 1632 after the death of his wife Mumtaz Mahal during childbirth, ordering a tomb built in white marble brought from Rajasthan along with inlaid gemstones sourced from as far as Afghanistan and Sri Lanka. Roughly 20,000 workers laboured on the site over the following two decades.

A popular story claims Shah Jahan had his workers' hands cut off afterward so the design could never be repeated, a tale with no contemporary evidence behind it. He was later deposed by his own son and spent his final years imprisoned in Agra Fort, from where he could see the tomb across the river.

Shah Jahan built the mausoleum for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631 giving birth to their fourteenth child. The main structure was largely finished by 1643, but the surrounding gardens, gateway and outbuildings kept craftsmen working for another decade, and 1653 is usually given as the year the whole complex was finally done.

Twenty thousand workers and craftsmen were brought in from across the Mughal empire and beyond, and the white marble was hauled from a quarry in Rajasthan, some 250 miles away, on a fleet of specially built carts and elephants. Shah Jahan was later buried beside Mumtaz Mahal in the same tomb he had spent decades having built for her.

The Tang court garrisoned outposts across the Tarim Basin and beyond to keep the Silk Road's oasis towns, places like Kucha and Khotan, open and taxable, turning a loose caravan route into something closer to a managed corridor backed by imperial soldiers and administrators.

That reach broke in 751 at the Battle of Talas, where Tang forces lost to an Abbasid army near the Talas River, and Tang influence in Central Asia contracted afterward. Chinese papermakers are said to have been among the prisoners taken, one route by which papermaking reached the Islamic world.

The Brihadeeswarar Temple's vimana, its tower over the main shrine, rises about 66 metres in thirteen tapering tiers, capped by a single dome-shaped stone weighing roughly eighty tonnes. How Chola builders lifted that block into place without cranes is still debated; one long-standing account describes a ramp built from a village several kilometres away to raise it gradually.

Rajaraja I completed the temple around 1010 to mark his conquests and to house a colossal stone lingam carved from a single piece of granite. For a time its tower was the tallest of its kind in India, a record eventually surpassed by later temple towers built under his successors and other South Indian dynasties.

Bankside Power Station stopped generating electricity in 1981 and sat empty on the Thames for over a decade before the Tate chose it over more than seventy other sites for a new gallery of international modern art. The architects Herzog and de Meuron kept the brick shell and the single central chimney almost untouched, gutting the turbine hall into a vast entrance space rather than disguising the building's industrial origin.

It opened in May 2000 and drew about 5.25 million visitors in its first year, far more than its planners had forecast, which forced an extension built over the following decade to add gallery space the original conversion had not budgeted for. The turbine hall itself became known for a running series of oversized temporary installations rather than paintings.

Dutch East India Company ships carried Chinese tea to Europe by around 1610, first as a curiosity sold in small quantities alongside porcelain and silk rather than as a staple cargo. It arrived decades before it caught on with any broad public, treated at first as a medicine reputed to settle the stomach.

England lagged behind the Dutch in the tea trade for most of the century, and it was British demand, once it finally took hold, that eventually reshaped the whole business: taxes on tea funded wars, smuggling networks grew around it, and by the 1700s the East India Company was importing it by the shipload rather than the chest.

Samuel Morse was not the first to build an electric telegraph; British inventors William Cooke and Charles Wheatstone had patented a working system in 1837 as well, and earlier experimental telegraphs existed before either. Morse's contribution, developed with Alfred Vail from 1837, paired a simple single wire system with a code of dots and dashes that was cheap to build and easy to learn.

Morse demonstrated his device to Congress and got funding in 1843 for a line between Washington and Baltimore, sending the message What hath God wrought when it opened the following year. The code and the low cost of his equipment let it spread across America and much of the world faster than the more elaborate British system.

Samuel Morse's original telegraph register scratched a paper tape with dots and dashes for an operator to read afterward, but skilled operators had noticed within a few years of the first lines opening in the 1840s that the clicking of the machine's arm already spelled out the message to a trained ear. Some were reading messages by sound rather than by tape well before any equipment was designed for it.

By around 1856 telegraph companies had adopted a purpose built sounder, a simpler device that produced a distinct click on and a click off with no moving pen or tape at all, letting an operator transcribe a message straight from the sound at speed. The sounder became the standard receiving instrument on American telegraph lines for the rest of the century, cheaper to run and faster to read than any recording register.

In the earliest telephone installations every subscriber's line ran directly to every other subscriber they wanted to call, which worked for a handful of connected offices but could not scale. George Coy, a telegraph man in New Haven, Connecticut, worked out that a switchboard could let an operator physically plug any caller's line into any other, and opened the first commercial exchange there on 28 January 1878.

The New Haven exchange served twenty one subscribers on its opening list, connected through a switchboard Coy improvised partly from carriage bolts and bustle wire. Within a few years telephone companies across the United States and Europe had copied the exchange model, and manual switchboards stayed the way calls were connected until automatic dial switching spread in the twentieth century.

Philo Farnsworth transmitted the first electronic television image, a simple line, from his San Francisco laboratory in September 1927, having sketched the idea for an image dissector tube as a teenager. He was still in his early twenties and largely self-taught, financing the work through investors who grew impatient waiting for a marketable product.

Farnsworth's claim to the invention was contested for years by RCA, whose researcher Vladimir Zworykin had filed an earlier patent application for a similar tube that did not yet work. A patent court eventually sided with Farnsworth in 1934, but RCA's marketing power meant it, not Farnsworth, dominated television's commercial rollout in the following decade.

A pilgrim could deposit money with the Knights Templar in London or Paris and draw an equivalent sum from a Templar house near Jerusalem, using a coded letter of credit instead of carrying coin along roads thick with bandits. By the mid 1100s the order ran roughly 900 houses across Europe and the Holy Land, enough to make that system work.

The Paris Temple doubled as a treasury for the French crown, and the order lent to kings as readily as to travellers, holding deposits and settling debts across borders. That financial reach, more than the knights themselves, is why Philip IV moved against the Templars in 1307, targeting an organisation he owed money to.

Seven columns are what remain, not the whole building. The Temple of Apollo at Corinth, raised around 540 BCE, replaced a 7th century predecessor destroyed by fire, and originally carried six columns at each short end and fifteen along each side, all cut as monolithic drums rather than stacked sections.

Those surviving seven are the oldest Doric columns still standing intact anywhere in mainland Greece, which is why the temple is treated as a benchmark for the order's early form: thick, squat shafts with almost no taper, built before Doric proportions settled into the leaner style seen later at Athens.

Construction on the Pyramid of the Sun at Teotihuacan began around 100 CE, using an estimated three million tonnes of rubble and adobe piled into a base wider than the Great Pyramid of Giza, though considerably lower at about 65 metres. The city that grew around it eventually held well over a hundred thousand people, making it one of the largest urban centres anywhere in the world at the time.

Beneath the pyramid, archaeologists found a natural cave system that may have been treated as sacred ground before construction started, suggesting the site was chosen rather than arbitrary. Teotihuacan's own name for the pyramid is unknown; Sun and Moon were labels the later Aztecs gave the abandoned ruins centuries after the city itself had collapsed.

Qin Shi Huang unified China's warring states in 221 BCE and then spent decades preparing a tomb complex near Xi'an that no one was meant to see. Around it, buried in pits, an army of over 8,000 life-size clay soldiers stood in battle formation, each face individually modelled, facing east toward the states he had conquered.

Farmers digging a well found the first fragments in 1974, more than two thousand years after burial. Excavation is still incomplete: the emperor's central tomb mound has never been opened, partly out of caution about preserving whatever lies inside once the seal is broken.

Filling the reservoir behind the Three Gorges Dam meant flooding thirteen cities, over a hundred towns and roughly 1,300 archaeological sites along the Yangtze, displacing more than a million people in a resettlement programme that ran across more than a decade of construction. The dam wall itself, over 2 kilometres wide and 181 metres tall, was completed in stages between 2003 and 2006 as the reservoir rose behind it.

By installed capacity it is the largest hydroelectric power station ever built, generating far more electricity than the Itaipu Dam on the Brazil-Paraguay border, its nearest rival by output. Its ship lift and locks were built partly to preserve river trade through the gorges that its own reservoir had submerged under water up to 175 metres deep.

Tikal's Great Plaza was rebuilt in stages for centuries before reaching the form visible today around 700, under rulers including Jasaw Chan Kawiil I, whose Temple I pyramid rises about 47 metres over the plaza's eastern side, facing the slightly shorter Temple II across the open space.

The city these temples anchored held an estimated population in the tens of thousands at its height, supported by reservoirs cut into the limestone bedrock to store rainwater through the dry season, since Tikal sits far from any permanent river or lake in the Guatemalan lowlands.

Forty one delegates from twenty six countries met in Washington from 1 October 1884, called at the request of President Chester Arthur to settle a single meridian for longitude and time. On 13 October they voted 22 to 1 for Greenwich, with San Domingo opposed and France and Brazil abstaining rather than concede the point to a British observatory.

France held out for years afterward, still describing its own time as Paris Mean Time retarded by nine minutes and twenty one seconds rather than say Greenwich outright. The conference fixed the reference line but left every country to decide when, or whether, to adopt standard zones, so the change reached railways and clocks unevenly over the following decades.

Tin ore is scarce and unevenly distributed, which makes its early history patchy by nature rather than poorly recorded. Cassiterite, the main tin ore, has been identified at early Bronze Age sites in Anatolia and central Asia, and analysis of bronze objects from around 3500 BCE shows tin alloyed with copper well before any written record names a mine.

Because workable tin deposits were rare, ancient bronze producers in Mesopotamia and the eastern Mediterranean depended on tin reaching them through long exchange networks rather than local mining alone. Trade routes later carried Cornish and central Asian tin thousands of kilometres to smiths who never saw the source, which is one reason tin, not copper, was the harder metal to keep supplied.

Cornish tin came mostly from streaming: gravel dug from riverbeds and washed to separate heavy ore, a method needing no deep shafts that left behind the pitted valley floors still visible in Cornwall today. By around 1200 this tin, alloyed with copper for bronze and with lead for pewter, was reaching markets across the English Channel.

Stannary courts in Devon and Cornwall were later chartered to regulate the trade, giving tin miners legal privileges separate from ordinary English law and their own coinage towns for weighing and taxing ore. The two counties together supplied a large share of medieval Europe's tin for centuries before those charters formalised the arrangement.

Tiwanaku sits at over 3,800 metres above sea level near the southern shore of Lake Titicaca, a height at which farming and large-scale building are both unusually hard. Its builders raised platform mounds and gateways from precisely cut stone blocks, some weighing many tonnes, fitted so closely that little or no mortar was needed.

The site's raised-field agriculture around the lake supported a population large enough to sustain long-distance building projects, and its influence spread through the southern Andes via trade and religious pilgrimage rather than conquest. Tiwanaku declined sharply after around 1000, likely tied to a prolonged drought that undermined the farming its monuments depended on.

Tula, the Toltec capital north of modern Mexico City, rose centuries after Teotihuacan's collapse but borrowed its architectural language, building stepped pyramids topped with colonnaded halls and, distinctively, rows of basalt warrior columns carved in relief, rather than plain stone piers.

Those warrior columns and feathered-serpent motifs turn up again at Chichen Itza hundreds of kilometres away, a resemblance close enough that historians still argue over whether Toltecs migrated there, traded ideas with it, or whether both cities simply drew on a shared older Mesoamerican tradition.

The Tui Tonga dynasty, based at Lapaha on Tongatapu, extended its influence toward Fiji and Samoa using double hulled sailing canoes capable of open ocean crossings of several hundred kilometres, navigated by stars, swells and bird flight rather than instruments. Stone tombs at Lapaha, built from coral slabs weighing several tonnes, mark the dynasty's centre.

Tribute in fine woven mats, red feathers and canoes moved along these routes toward Tonga, tying islands hundreds of kilometres apart into one political network by around 1200. That reach later drew comparisons to a maritime empire, though it rested on kinship and tribute obligations rather than standing garrisons or fortresses.

Tower Bridge opened on 30 June 1894 after eight years of construction, built to ease traffic across the Thames without blocking tall ships heading for the busy docks upstream of London Bridge. Its solution was a bascule design: two roadway sections that hinge upward on hydraulic machinery, originally powered by steam engines that were only replaced with electric pumps in 1976.

The stone Gothic towers are largely decorative, clad around a steel frame chosen so the bridge would match the nearby Tower of London rather than look like the industrial ironwork it actually is. In 1952 a bus driver had to accelerate across a gap as the bascules began to rise beneath him after a signalling error, an incident the bridge's operators still cite in staff training.

William the Conqueror began the White Tower around 1078 to overawe a recently conquered London, using imported Caen stone from Normandy rather than local materials, a deliberate display that the new rulers could command resources across the Channel. The fortress grew over subsequent reigns into the concentric castle of walls and towers that stands today.

Its uses ranged far beyond defence: it held the royal mint, an armoury, a menagerie that once included lions and a polar bear, and a prison whose inmates included Anne Boleyn and, centuries later, Rudolf Hess. The Crown Jewels have been kept there since the seventeenth century.

A continuous carved frieze spirals up the column for roughly 190 metres, wrapping it 23 times to tell the story of Trajan's wars against Dacia in modern Romania. Originally the scenes were painted in colour, and a bronze statue of the emperor stood on top until it was lost in the Middle Ages and replaced with a statue of Saint Peter in 1588.

The column doubled as a tomb: a chamber at its base once held a golden urn with Trajan's ashes. Later emperors used it as a model rather than a rival, and Rome's other great carved column, the Column of Marcus Aurelius, borrowed the same spiral format decades afterward.

Aramco built the pipeline, known as Tapline, to avoid shipping Saudi crude the long way around Arabia by tanker through the Persian Gulf and Suez. It ran roughly 1,650 kilometres from the oilfields near Abqaiq across Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Syria to the Lebanese port of Sidon on the Mediterranean, cutting the journey to European markets by weeks.

Tapline created towns and jobs along a route that had previously been mostly desert track, and it operated for over four decades. Repeated closures from regional conflict and disputes over transit fees eroded its usefulness, and the line was finally shut down for good in 1990.

The main line between Moscow and Vladivostok opened in July 1904 after thirteen years of construction ordered by Tsar Alexander III, running roughly 9,300 kilometres and remaining the longest single railway line in the world today. Convict and exile labour built long stretches of it through Siberian forest and permafrost, in conditions that killed workers from cold, disease and rockfalls.

Work continued for over a decade after the 1904 opening, including a shorter route around Lake Baikal that replaced an earlier ferry crossing and a bridge over the Amur River finished only in 1916. The railway allowed Russia to move troops and settlers east far faster than before, reshaping Siberia's economy within a generation.

Architect William Pereira gave the Transamerica Pyramid its tapered shape in 1972 partly to let more daylight and open sky reach the streets below, rather than casting the dense shadow a boxy tower of the same height would. At 260 metres it became San Francisco's tallest building on completion, a title it held for decades before being overtaken by the Salesforce Tower in 2018.

Two narrow wings jut from the sides near the top, housing an elevator shaft and a smoking lounge, the only parts of the tower that break its otherwise unbroken pyramid outline. Locals and the press mocked the design as a joke before it opened, but the building became one of the city's most photographed landmarks, appearing in its official seal alongside the Golden Gate Bridge.

The ship Great Eastern left Valentia Island, Ireland, in July 1866 carrying over 2,700 nautical miles of cable, and reached Heart's Content, Newfoundland, fourteen days later with a working line. It was not the first attempt: an 1858 cable had briefly connected the continents before failing within weeks, and an 1865 attempt had snapped and been lost at sea.

The 1866 cable carried messages at roughly eight words a minute, slow by later standards but eighty times faster than its 1858 predecessor. The Great Eastern then went back, recovered the lost 1865 cable from the seabed, spliced it, and completed it too, so that by September two working lines crossed the Atlantic instead of none.

On 10 May 1869 the Central Pacific and Union Pacific lines met at Promontory Summit, Utah, where a ceremonial golden spike was driven into a polished laurel tie. The Central Pacific's track east from California relied heavily on Chinese immigrant labourers, who cut through the Sierra Nevada by hand and black powder, often in winter conditions that killed dozens.

The link cut the journey between the coasts from months by wagon to about a week by train, and it reshaped where towns and industries grew along its route. Promontory Summit itself, chosen partly for convenience, was later bypassed by a shorter route across the Great Salt Lake and today survives mainly as a historic site.

Harry Beck was an engineering draughtsman for London's Underground, laid off between contracts in 1931, when he sketched a map on his own time that threw out geography. Stations sat at even spacing along lines bent to verticals, horizontals and forty five degree diagonals, with only the Thames kept as a landmark.

His employers turned it down as too radical for a first run and printed a small trial batch instead. Passengers liked what the planners doubted: about 850,000 pocket copies went out in the first two months of 1933, and Beck kept redrawing the map himself until 1959, long after its lines outnumbered the ones he started with.

Tulum's own name may not be its original one. Some sources give it as Zama, meaning city of dawn, for its position facing the sunrise off a limestone cliff; Tulum, meaning wall or fence, was likely adopted later for the barrier that still runs some four hundred metres along the landward side, three to five metres high with watchtowers at two corners.

It was one of the last Maya cities still occupied when Europeans reached the coast: a member of Juan de Grijalva's 1518 expedition recorded seeing it, its walls and temples visible from the sea. As a port it fed goods inland to Coba, forty two kilometres away, moving jade, obsidian, cotton and cacao through a narrow reef gap below the cliffs.

Eupalinos built his tunnel around 530 BCE to bring water from a spring on the far side of a mountain into the fortified city of Samos, keeping the pipeline hidden from any besieging enemy who might otherwise cut it off. The finished passage ran 1,036 metres straight through solid rock.

Two crews dug from opposite ends at once, using geometry to keep both headings aimed correctly with no way to check progress against the surface above. When they met in the middle, the two tunnels were offset by only about 60 centimetres in height, an accuracy that would be difficult even with today's basic instruments, let alone the sightlines and rods Eupalinos had.

The Gur-e-Amir was not built for the man it is now known for. Work began in 1403 after the sudden death of Muhammad Sultan, Timur's grandson and chosen heir, and the mausoleum was meant for him. When Timur himself died in early 1405, on campaign in Kazakhstan, he was brought back to Samarkand and buried in the same tomb built for his grandson.

Its ribbed dome, thirty two metres high and covered in blue tile, was finished by 1404, though the finer exterior tilework continued for roughly another decade. Timur's body was later examined in 1941 by Soviet archaeologists, whose findings confirmed a leg injury matching the accounts of his lameness and settled long-standing arguments over which set of remains in the crypt was actually his.

Eero Saarinen never called his TWA terminal a bird, though the comparison stuck the moment it opened at Idlewild Airport, later renamed JFK, in 1962. The four vaulted concrete shells rise and curve toward the sky, and inside there is barely a straight line: the ticket counters, staircases and even the departure boards were custom-shaped to match the building's flow rather than fitted into it afterward.

Saarinen died of a brain tumour in 1961, a year before the terminal opened, and never saw it in use. Jet-age airliners soon outgrew the gates he had designed for propeller planes and early jets, and the building stopped handling flights in 2001. It reopened in 2019 as a hotel, its shells preserved as the lobby rather than demolished for a larger terminal.

John D. Rockefeller Jr. bought the East River site, a former slaughterhouse and rail yard district, and donated it to the United Nations after the organisation's search for a home elsewhere had stalled. An international team of architects worked under Wallace Harrison, including Le Corbusier and Oscar Niemeyer, though their competing visions for the site produced friction Harrison had to resolve himself.

The Secretariat tower, a slab of glass and marble finished in 1950, became a template copied by office buildings worldwide long before the wider complex was finished in 1952. The land the UN sits on is technically international territory, not part of New York City, though it remains subject to most local laws by agreement.

The staircase now most associated with the Vatican Museums was designed by engineer Giuseppe Momo in 1932, not by Donato Bramante, whose separate and much older square spiral staircase from around 1505 sits elsewhere in the palace and is often confused with it. Momo's version consists of two ramps wound around a single shaft in a double helix, so people can climb and descend without ever meeting on the stairs.

Its ironwork balustrade and terracotta-coloured steps were built to serve as the museums' grand exit, letting large crowds leave in one continuous flow rather than queuing on a single staircase. Photographers now treat it as one of the most recognisable images inside the Vatican, framed from directly above to show the two spirals nesting around each other.

A ribbed vault splits the weight of a ceiling onto a skeleton of stone arches, leaving the spaces between them as thin infill rather than solid masonry. That shift, worked out in northern French workshops in the twelfth century, is what let architects around 1200 raise ceilings far higher than the rounded Romanesque vaults they replaced.

Surviving masons' drawings from Reims and the notebook of Villard de Honnecourt, made in the 1220s and 1230s, show the geometry worked out on paper before a single stone was cut, templates and all. That planning discipline is the clearest surviving evidence of how the technique spread from one cathedral site to the next.

NASA finished the Vehicle Assembly Building at Kennedy Space Center in 1966 to stack Saturn V rockets vertically before rolling them to the launch pad on a crawler. At 160 metres it was built tall enough to enclose a fully assembled Saturn V, engine to nose cone, with room above for the overhead cranes that lifted each stage into place.

The building is so large that its interior air handling has to fight condensation forming under its own roof on humid Florida days, effectively generating indoor weather. Giant American flag and NASA logo panels painted on its exterior are each roughly the size of a basketball court, a scale chosen so the markings would still register from miles away across the flat Florida scrubland.

No inventor's name attaches to the verge escapement, and no single dated document announces it. Historians place its appearance in the late thirteenth century because that is when written references to clocks that regulate themselves, rather than simply run down under a falling weight, start appearing in cathedral and monastery accounts.

The mechanism swings a bar back and forth between two teeth on a rotating wheel, converting a steady pull into a ticking rhythm that a bell or a sundial could never give. It stayed the standard regulator in tower clocks and, later, watches for nearly six centuries, only giving way once the pendulum and then the balance spring offered steadier timekeeping.

When the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge opened on 21 November 1964, its main span of 1,298 metres beat the Golden Gate Bridge by about 18 metres, making it briefly the longest suspension span on earth. Robert Moses pushed the project through against opposition from residents of Bay Ridge and Staten Island, whose neighbourhoods lost hundreds of homes to the approaches.

The bridge's twin towers are almost four centimetres further apart at the top than at the base, a gap engineers had to build in deliberately because the earth's curvature pulls two tall, parallel verticals slightly out of true. It held the world record for 17 years, until England's Humber Bridge overtook it in 1981, and it is still the longest suspension bridge in the Americas.

Before 1661 Versailles was a modest brick and stone hunting lodge that Louis XIV's father Louis XIII had built south west of Paris. The young king expanded it repeatedly rather than starting from a plan, adding envelope wings around the old lodge in the 1660s and then the vast north and south wings decades later under the architect Jules Hardouin Mansart.

The building work never really stopped in Louis XIV's lifetime, running alongside the gardens, canals and fountains that consumed a comparable share of the budget. The court did not move there permanently until 1682, more than twenty years after the first digging began, by which point thousands of labourers, some conscripted from the army, had been employed on the site.

Versailles began as Louis XIII's modest hunting lodge, a place his son had no fondness for at first. Louis XIV rebuilt it into a seat of government almost out of spite for Paris, where he had lived through the frightening street uprisings of the Fronde as a child, and by 1682 he moved his entire court and administration there permanently.

The move put roughly three thousand nobles, courtiers and officials under one roof, alongside thousands more servants, and turned attendance at Versailles into a political necessity: a nobleman who stayed away lost influence at court. Louis used the palace's rigid daily ceremonies, dressing and dining in public, to keep the aristocracy watched and occupied rather than plotting in their own provinces.

Nero had drained an artificial lake south of the Palatine to build the grounds of his Golden House, a private estate carved out of land burned in the great fire of 64. Vespasian chose that exact spot in 72 to start his amphitheatre, replacing an emperor's pleasure gardens with a building meant for the whole city.

Money for the project came from the spoils of the Jewish War, which Vespasian and his son Titus had just finished putting down in Judaea. Vespasian did not live to see it open; he died in 79, a year before Titus dedicated the finished amphitheatre with games that reportedly ran for a hundred days.

Krishna Deva Raya, who ruled Vijayanagara from 1509 to 1529, financed temple building at a scale the empire had not managed before, funded largely by control of the inland cotton and spice trade and by war plunder from campaigns against neighbouring Deccan sultanates. The Vitthala temple complex at Hampi, with its stone chariot and musical pillars, dates mainly from his reign.

Portuguese travellers who visited Hampi during Krishna Deva Raya's rule described a city larger and richer than Rome, crowded with markets selling diamonds by the roadside. That prosperity ended abruptly in 1565, when a coalition of Deccan sultanates defeated Vijayanagara at Talikota and sacked the capital over several months, leaving the temple ruins that survive today.

Rival Dutch trading firms had been undercutting each other in Asian markets for years before the States General forced them into one company in 1602, granting it a monopoly on Dutch trade east of the Cape of Good Hope and the power to wage war, build forts and sign treaties in its own name. Shares traded on the Amsterdam exchange, the first time ordinary investors could buy a stake in a venture without joining a single voyage.

Its charter let it act as a private state: the VOC ran its own courts and armed fleets across Asia, and by the 1660s it had seized most Portuguese trading posts in the region. Mismanagement and war debts caught up with it, and the company was dissolved in 1799 with its Asian territories passed directly to the Dutch government.

Rendering blubber into oil produced a fuel that burned cleaner and brighter than tallow candles, and by the mid-1600s colonial ports on Long Island and Nantucket had built their economies around it, sending small boats after whales that passed close to shore. Right whales, slow and easy to approach, were hunted first and were nearly gone from those coastal waters within a few decades.

Sperm whale oil, discovered to burn even more cleanly, pushed voyages further out to sea and eventually across whole oceans, turning a shore trade into a hunt that could last years per ship. Petroleum kerosene undercut whale oil's price in the 1850s and 1860s, and that competition, not any deliberate conservation effort, did most of the work of ending commercial whale oil's dominance in lighting.

Irish architect James Hoban won a design competition for the presidential residence, and construction ran from 1792 to 1800 using enslaved and free labourers alongside European stonemasons. John Adams became the first president to live there in November 1800, moving into a building whose plaster was still drying and whose grounds were still a construction site.

The sandstone exterior was originally whitewashed with a lime mixture to protect it from moisture, which is where its familiar colour came from long before it carried the name officially. British troops burned the interior during the War of 1812, and Hoban was brought back to rebuild it, reopening it for James Monroe in 1817.

The Winter Palace on the Neva was the fourth palace built on or near the site for the Romanovs, designed by Bartolomeo Rastrelli for Empress Elizabeth and finished in 1762, the year she died without seeing it in use. It housed roughly 1,500 rooms and became the official winter residence of the Russian tsars for the century and a half that followed.

It was here that a crowd of unarmed petitioners was fired on by troops in 1905, an event remembered as Bloody Sunday, and it was the Provisional Government's seat when Bolshevik forces stormed it in October 1917. The palace now forms the core of the State Hermitage Museum, one of the largest art collections in the world.

Edward I needed money for wars in Wales and Scotland, and English wool, spun into cloth by Flemish weavers who had no comparable supply of their own, was the crown's most reliable source of it. The Great Custom of 1275, agreed with merchants rather than simply imposed, set a fixed export duty on every sack of wool leaving English ports.

The duty was collected at a handful of designated ports and staple towns, which made it far easier to enforce than a tax on scattered inland trade would have been. Wool duties went on to fund a large share of royal revenue for the rest of the medieval period, and the staple system built around collecting them shaped English trade policy for generations after Edward's death.

Edward III did not invent the staple to help merchants. His Great Council issued the Ordinance of the Staple in October 1353 mainly so the crown could actually collect the tax owed on England's most valuable export, by forcing every bale of raw wool through a short list of named ports where customs officers were already stationed. The following year's statute named fifteen towns, among them London, York, Bristol and Dublin.

The list did not stay fixed. In 1363 the crown moved the staple to Calais, on the French side of the Channel, and granted a company of English merchants known as the Staplers a lucrative monopoly over the trade passing through it. Wool duties became one of the crown's most reliable sources of income for the rest of the century, which is why the system kept being renewed rather than abandoned.

Construction on the World Trade Center's twin towers began in August 1968 on landfill created from the excavated site itself, soil and rock dug out for the foundations dumped into the Hudson River to extend Manhattan's shoreline by several blocks. The towers used a then-unusual tube structure, with steel columns packed close along the exterior walls taking the load rather than a dense internal skeleton.

Minoru Yamasaki designed narrow windows just 45 centimetres wide, partly for structural reasons and partly because he was uneasy with heights himself and wanted occupants to feel enclosed rather than exposed. The North Tower topped out in 1970 and the South Tower in 1971, and together they briefly held the title of the world's tallest building before Chicago's Sears Tower overtook them in 1973.

The medieval St Paul's had already been decaying for decades when the Great Fire of 1666 gutted what was left of it, melting the lead roof and cracking the stone. Christopher Wren's first replacement design, a Greek cross under a single dome, was rejected by the clergy as too radical, and the version he began building from 1675 kept a more traditional long nave to satisfy them.

Wren then quietly altered the design as construction went on, adding the drum and dome largely on his own authority once building was underway, protected by a royal warrant that let him make changes without further approval. The cathedral was declared finished in 1710, thirty five years after work started, and Wren lived to see it complete.

Iron made with mineral coal picked up sulphur and other impurities that made it too brittle to forge, so ironmasters had kept relying on charcoal, a fuel growing scarce and expensive. Henry Cort's puddling furnace, patented in 1784, kept the molten iron separate from the coal fire while a worker stirred, or puddled, the metal with a long rod to burn off carbon and expose it evenly to the air.

The result was wrought iron strong enough for the process to be paired with grooved rollers, also patented by Cort, that squeezed out slag and shaped the iron into bars far faster than a hammer could. Puddling and rolling together let British iron output multiply within a generation, feeding the machinery, rails and ships of the Industrial Revolution, though the fumes made puddling one of the era's harshest trades.

Kublai Khan had moved the capital north to Beijing, a city with no direct river link to the rice-growing Yangtze delta that fed it. The older Grand Canal looped far to the west through Kaifeng, a detour the Mongol court had no patience for, so Yuan engineers cut new sections straight across Shandong between 1283 and 1289 to shorten the route by hundreds of kilometres.

The realigned canal needed dozens of locks and a summit crossing to climb over Shandong's watershed, engineering that later Ming and Qing dynasties maintained rather than redesigned. Grain barges could then reach Beijing largely by inland water, reducing the empire's dependence on the coastal sea route, which pirates and storms had made unreliable for large shipments.

King Ur-Nammu began the Great Ziggurat of Ur around 2100 BCE as a stepped mud-brick platform for a shrine to the moon god Nanna, set at the top rather than inside the structure itself. The core was built of sun-dried mud brick, faced with fired brick set in bitumen to shed rain, a construction detail that let much of it survive.

The building fell into ruin over the following centuries until Nabonidus, Babylon's last king, restored it in the sixth century BCE. British archaeologist Leonard Woolley excavated and partially reconstructed the lower stages in the 1920s, and its restored silhouette is largely his interpretation rather than the untouched original.
